docs.title: 1.22 — Anonymous Types, dynamic, and var
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.21 IDisposable · Next: 1.23 Attributes and reflection

Markers: — · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• var is still fully type-safe. The compiler works out the type and fixes it. var x = 5; and int x = 5; produce identical code.
  • dynamic genuinely turns off type checking until runtime. Everything becomes a runtime error waiting to happen.
  • Anonymous types (new { Name = "Ada" }) are real, compiler-generated classes. Useful inside a method, useless outside one.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
These three get grouped together because they all look like "the type is not specified". Only one of them actually is.

  • var — "compiler, work out the type for me". Type safety is completely intact.
  • dynamic — "do not check anything, sort it out at runtime". Type safety is gone.
  • anonymous type — "make me a throwaway class here and now".

The interview question is almost always var versus dynamic. The answer is that they are not remotely similar, and confusing them is a red flag.

docs.title: var — type inference
docs.text:
The compiler looks at the right-hand side and works out the type. Once it has, that type is fixed forever.

var number = 5;              // compiler decides: int
var name = "Ada";            // compiler decides: string
var list = new List<Order>();// compiler decides: List<Order>

number = "hello";            // COMPILE ERROR — number is an int, permanently

var x = 5; and int x = 5; compile to exactly the same IL. There is no runtime cost and no loss of safety. var is purely about how much you type.

Rules:

  • Only for local variables. Not for fields, parameters, or return types.
  • You must initialise it in the same statement — the compiler needs something to infer from.
  • Cannot be null on its own: var x = null; fails, because null does not identify a type.

When to use it is a style question, and teams differ. A reasonable position:

var order = new Order();                       // obvious — the type is right there
var orders = new List<Dictionary<string, int>>();  // obvious, and saves a lot of typing

var result = ProcessThings();                  // NOT obvious — what does this return?
IReadOnlyList<Order> result = ProcessThings(); // clearer

The test: can a reader tell the type from this one line? If yes, var is fine. If they would have to go and look at the method signature, write the type out.

docs.title: dynamic — no compile-time checking at all
docs.text:
dynamic value = GetSomething();
value.AnyMethodAtAll();          // compiles fine, whatever it is
value.ThisDoesNotExist();        // ALSO compiles fine
                                 // → RuntimeBinderException when it runs

The compiler stops checking entirely. Member lookup happens while the program is running, using the Dynamic Language Runtime.

The costs are real:

  • No compile-time errors. Every typo becomes a runtime crash.
  • No IntelliSense. Your editor cannot help you.
  • Slower. Every call goes through a lookup and caching mechanism.
  • No refactoring safety. Rename a property and dynamic call sites are silently missed.

When is it justified? Genuinely rarely:

  • Talking to COM objects, like Office automation
  • Interoperating with a dynamic language such as IronPython
  • Truly unknown JSON shapes — though JsonNode or JsonElement is usually better

If you find yourself reaching for dynamic in normal application code, there is almost always a better answer: an interface, a generic, or pattern matching.

docs.title: dynamic vs object vs var
docs.text:
This comparison is a common question:

object o = "hello";
o.Length;              // COMPILE ERROR — object has no Length. Cast first.

dynamic d = "hello";
d.Length;              // Compiles. Works at runtime. Returns 5.
d.Nonsense();          // Compiles. Throws at runtime.

var v = "hello";
v.Length;              // Compiles. v IS a string — full IntelliSense.
v.Nonsense();          // COMPILE ERROR — caught immediately.
Checked at compile time? Needs a cast? IntelliSense? var Yes No Yes object Yes Yes No, until cast dynamic No No No

docs.title: Anonymous types
docs.text:
var person = new { Name = "Ada", Age = 36 };
Console.WriteLine(person.Name);      // fully typed, IntelliSense works

The compiler generates a real class behind the scenes with read-only properties, a value-based Equals and GetHashCode, and a helpful ToString.

Their limitation is that the type has no name you can write. So you cannot return one from a method, put one in a field, or use it as a parameter type. It only works inside the method that created it — which is exactly why var is required for them.

Their main real use is LINQ projections:

var summary = orders
    .Where(o => o.Total > 100)
    .Select(o => new { o.Id, o.CustomerName, o.Total })   // only these 3 columns
    .ToList();

In Entity Framework this is genuinely useful, because it means the generated SQL only selects the three columns you actually need instead of the whole row. See 13.15.

But once the data leaves the method, use a record instead:

public record OrderSummary(Guid Id, string CustomerName, decimal Total);

public IReadOnlyList<OrderSummary> GetSummaries() =>
    _db.Orders
       .Where(o => o.Total > 100)
       .Select(o => new OrderSummary(o.Id, o.Customer.Name, o.Total))
       .ToList();

Same SQL benefit, but now it has a name, it can be returned, and it appears properly in Swagger.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between var and dynamic?

They are completely different despite looking similar. var is compile-time type inference — the compiler works out the type from the initialiser and fixes it permanently, so you get full type checking, IntelliSense and no runtime cost at all. var x = 5; compiles to exactly the same thing as int x = 5;. dynamic switches type checking off entirely: member lookup is deferred to runtime, so any typo compiles fine and throws when it executes, there is no IntelliSense, and every call has overhead. var is about convenience; dynamic is about giving up safety, and it is rarely the right choice.

Q: When is dynamic actually appropriate?

When the type genuinely is not known until runtime and there is no reasonable alternative — COM interop like automating Excel, interoperating with a dynamic language, or handling completely unstructured data. Even for JSON, JsonNode or JsonElement is usually a better answer because it gives you a real API. In ordinary application code, reaching for dynamic is normally a sign that an interface or a generic would solve the problem properly.

Q: What is an anonymous type and where would you use one?

It is a compiler-generated class created inline with new { Name = "Ada" }. The compiler produces a real type with read-only properties and value-based equality, but that type has no name you can write, so it cannot leave the method it was created in. That makes them useful for LINQ projections — selecting only the three columns you need from a query so that Entity Framework generates narrower SQL. As soon as the data needs to cross a method boundary, a record is the better choice, because it has a name, it can be returned, and it shows up properly in API documentation.

Q: Does var have any runtime cost?

None at all. It is purely a compile-time convenience. The compiler determines the concrete type and emits exactly the same IL as if you had typed the type out yourself. The variable is just as strongly typed either way.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Thinking var is weakly typed. It is not. The type is fixed at compile time.
  • dynamic turns every typo into a runtime crash. No compiler help, no IntelliSense, no safe refactoring.
  • Overusing var hurts readability. var result = Process(); tells a reader nothing.
  • Anonymous types cannot escape the method. No returning them, no fields, no parameters.
  • Anonymous type equality is by value, but only for the exact same shape. Two anonymous types with the same properties in a different order are different types.
  • dynamic silently defeats extension methods. Extension methods are resolved at compile time, so calling one on a dynamic fails at runtime.
  • var x = null; does not compile. You need string? x = null; or a cast.

docs.title: 1.23 — Attributes and Reflection
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.22 Anonymous types, dynamic, var · Next: 1.24 Partial classes and local functions

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• An attribute is a label you attach to code. On its own it does nothing — something has to go looking for it.
  • Reflection is code inspecting types at runtime: finding attributes, reading properties, calling methods by name.
  • Reflection is slow and unsafe at compile time. Cache what you look up, and prefer source generators when you can.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
An attribute is a sticky note on your code.

[Required]
public string Name { get; set; }

That [Required] does absolutely nothing by itself. It does not validate anything. It is just a note stored in the compiled file saying "this property has been marked Required".

Something else — the ASP.NET Core validation system — comes along later, looks at the property, finds the note, and acts on it.

Reflection is the mechanism for reading those notes, and more generally for a program to examine itself at runtime: listing a type's properties, finding its methods, creating instances, and calling things by name.

Together they are how a huge amount of ASP.NET Core works. Attributes describe intent; the framework uses reflection to discover it.

docs.title: Attributes you already use
docs.text:
[ApiController]
[Route("api/[controller]")]
public class OrdersController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet("{id:guid}")]
    [Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]
    [ProducesResponseType<OrderDto>(StatusCodes.Status200OK)]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Get(Guid id) { }
}

public class CreateOrderRequest
{
    [Required]
    [StringLength(100, MinimumLength = 3)]
    public string CustomerName { get; set; } = "";

    [Range(0.01, 100_000)]
    public decimal Total { get; set; }
}

Every one of those brackets is a note. None of them contains logic. The routing system, the authorization system, the validation system and Swagger each read the ones they care about.

docs.title: Writing your own attribute
docs.text:
[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Property, AllowMultiple = false)]
public class SensitiveAttribute(string reason) : Attribute
{
    public string Reason { get; } = reason;
}

public class Customer
{
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";

    [Sensitive("PII — must be redacted in logs")]
    public string Email { get; set; } = "";
}

Two conventions worth knowing:

  • The class name ends in Attribute, but you leave that off when using it. SensitiveAttribute is written as [Sensitive].
  • [AttributeUsage] controls where it can be applied and whether it can appear more than once. Without it, your attribute can go anywhere, which is rarely what you want.

docs.title: Reflection — reading the notes
docs.text:
var properties = typeof(Customer).GetProperties();

foreach (var prop in properties)
{
    var sensitive = prop.GetCustomAttribute<SensitiveAttribute>();
    if (sensitive is not null)
        Console.WriteLine($"{prop.Name} is sensitive: {sensitive.Reason}");
}

// Output: Email is sensitive: PII — must be redacted in logs

Other things reflection can do:

var type = typeof(Customer);

type.Name;                                  // "Customer"
type.GetProperties();                       // all public properties
type.GetMethods();                          // all public methods

var instance = Activator.CreateInstance(type);      // create one by type
var instance2 = Activator.CreateInstance<Customer>();

var prop = type.GetProperty("Email");
prop?.SetValue(instance, "a@b.com");        // set a property by name
var value = prop?.GetValue(instance);       // read it back

var method = type.GetMethod("Validate");
method?.Invoke(instance, null);             // call a method by name

Notice how much of this is string-based. GetProperty("Email") returns null if you misspell it or someone renames the property — no compile error, and rename refactoring will not update the string. That is the fundamental danger of reflection.

docs.title: The performance problem
docs.text:
Reflection is slow. Roughly speaking, calling a method through reflection is hundreds of times slower than calling it directly, because every call has to look up metadata, check access, and box the arguments.

If you must use it, cache the lookup:

// BAD — does the expensive lookup on every single call
public string GetName(object obj)
    => obj.GetType().GetProperty("Name")?.GetValue(obj)?.ToString() ?? "";

// BETTER — look it up once per type, then reuse
private static readonly ConcurrentDictionary<Type, PropertyInfo?> _cache = new();

public string GetName(object obj)
{
    var prop = _cache.GetOrAdd(obj.GetType(), t => t.GetProperty("Name"));
    return prop?.GetValue(obj)?.ToString() ?? "";
}

The lookup is the expensive part. The invoke is much cheaper. Caching PropertyInfo objects turns a slow operation into a reasonable one.

docs.title: The modern alternative — source generators
docs.text:
Reflection does its work at runtime. A source generator does the same kind of work at compile time, writing real C# code into your project that the compiler then compiles normally.

That gives you three wins at once: no runtime cost, full compile-time checking, and it works with Native AOT (which trims away unused types, breaking reflection).

This is why modern .NET has been moving away from reflection:

// Source-generated JSON — no reflection at runtime
[JsonSerializable(typeof(Order))]
internal partial class OrderJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext { }

var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, OrderJsonContext.Default.Order);

The same shift has happened for logging ([LoggerMessage]), regular expressions ([GeneratedRegex]), and configuration binding. Mentioning this trend is a good way to show you follow modern .NET. See 21.13.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic use — automatically redacting sensitive fields before logging:

public static class LogSanitizer
{
    // Cache the reflection work per type. Done once, reused forever.
    private static readonly ConcurrentDictionary<Type, PropertyInfo[]> _sensitiveProps = new();

    public static Dictionary<string, object?> ToLogSafeDictionary(object obj)
    {
        var type = obj.GetType();

        var sensitive = _sensitiveProps.GetOrAdd(type, t =>
            t.GetProperties()
             .Where(p => p.GetCustomAttribute<SensitiveAttribute>() is not null)
             .ToArray());

        var sensitiveNames = sensitive.Select(p => p.Name).ToHashSet();

        return type.GetProperties()
            .ToDictionary(
                p => p.Name,
                p => sensitiveNames.Contains(p.Name)
                        ? "***REDACTED***"
                        : p.GetValue(obj));
    }
}

The pattern here is the one to remember: do the reflection once per type and cache it, then the per-call work is just a dictionary lookup.

See 18.10 for why redacting matters.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is an attribute?

It is metadata attached to code — a class, method, property or parameter. On its own it does nothing at all; it is just information stored in the compiled assembly. Something else has to read it and act on it, usually through reflection. [Required] does not validate anything by itself — ASP.NET Core's validation system finds it and applies the rule. That separation is the whole design: attributes describe intent, and a framework decides what to do about it.

Q: What is reflection and what is it used for?

It is the ability of code to inspect and manipulate types at runtime — listing properties and methods, reading attributes, creating instances, and invoking members by name. It is what makes most frameworks possible. ASP.NET Core uses it to discover controllers and map routes, the DI container uses it to work out constructor parameters, serializers use it to map JSON to properties, and ORMs use it to map rows to entities.

Q: What are the downsides of reflection?

Three main ones. It is slow — a reflective call is orders of magnitude more expensive than a direct one, because of metadata lookup, access checks and boxing. It is not type-safe, since you are usually looking things up by string, so a typo or a rename becomes a runtime failure with no compiler warning. And it breaks with trimming and Native AOT, because the compiler cannot see which types are used and removes them. The mitigations are to cache the metadata lookups, and increasingly to use source generators, which do the equivalent work at compile time with none of the drawbacks.

Q: What is a source generator and how does it relate to this?

It is a compiler plugin that generates real C# source code during compilation, which is then compiled normally. It solves the same problems reflection solves, but at build time — so there is no runtime cost, everything is checked by the compiler, and it works under Native AOT. Modern .NET has been steadily replacing reflection with source generators for JSON serialization, logging, regular expressions and configuration binding.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Attributes do nothing by themselves. If nothing reads it, it has no effect. A custom attribute with no handler is a very confusing no-op.
  • Reflection is slow — but the lookup is the slow part. Cache PropertyInfo and MethodInfo; do not re-fetch on every call.
  • String-based lookups break silently on rename. nameof() helps where you can use it.
  • Reflection can reach private members. Convenient in tests, but it means private is not a security boundary.
  • Reflection breaks under trimming and Native AOT. Types that are only referenced reflectively get removed, and you get a runtime failure that never happened in debug.
  • GetCustomAttribute returns a new instance each time by default. Do not rely on reference equality between calls.
  • Attribute arguments must be compile-time constants. You cannot pass a computed value or a DateTime.

docs.title: 1.24 — Partial Classes, Partial Methods, Local Functions
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.23 Attributes and reflection · Next: 1.25 Span and Memory

Markers: — · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• partial lets one class be split across several files. It exists mainly so generated code and your code can live in the same class without overwriting each other.
  • A local function is a method declared inside another method. It is faster than a lambda and can be called before it is declared.
  • Prefer a local function over a lambda for a private helper — and mark it static if it does not need anything from around it.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Both of these are about organising code, not about new capability.

partial answers: "how do I have both hand-written and machine-generated code in the same class, without the generator wiping out my work every time it runs?"

Local functions answer: "I need a small helper that only this one method uses — where do I put it so it does not clutter the class?"

docs.title: Partial classes
docs.text:
Add partial to a class and you can split it across as many files as you like. The compiler joins them back into one class.

// Order.cs — your hand-written code
public partial class Order
{
    public void ApplyDiscount(decimal percent) { /* ... */ }
}

// Order.Generated.cs — written by a tool
public partial class Order
{
    public Guid Id { get; set; }
    public decimal Total { get; set; }
}

At compile time these become one class with all four members. Neither file knows about the other.

Rules: every part needs partial, they must all be in the same assembly and namespace, and accessibility must match.

Where you will actually meet this:

  • Razor Pages — the .cshtml file and its .cshtml.cs code-behind are two halves of one partial class
  • EF Core scaffolding from an existing database
  • Blazor components
  • Source generators, which need somewhere to put the code they write

Where not to use it: splitting your own class across files because it got too big. A class that needs three files to hold it is a class doing too much. Splitting it up hides the problem instead of fixing it.

docs.title: Partial methods
docs.text:
A partial method is declared in one part and optionally implemented in another:

public partial class Order
{
    public void Complete()
    {
        Status = OrderStatus.Complete;
        OnCompleted();          // a hook
    }

    partial void OnCompleted();   // declared, maybe never implemented
}

The clever bit: if nobody implements OnCompleted, the compiler removes the call entirely. There is no empty method call at runtime, no cost at all.

This is how generated code offers extension points. The tool writes the hook; you implement it only if you need it.

Since C# 9, partial methods can also have a return value and be public, but then an implementation becomes mandatory — the compiler cannot silently remove a call that produces a value someone is using.

docs.title: Local functions
docs.text:
A method declared inside another method:

public IEnumerable<int> GetFactors(int number)
{
    ValidateInput();                       // called before it is declared — fine

    for (var i = 1; i <= number; i++)
        if (number % i == 0)
            yield return i;

    void ValidateInput()                   // declared at the bottom
    {
        if (number <= 0)
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(number));
    }
}

Two things worth noting. You can call it before it is declared, unlike a local variable — so you can put helpers at the bottom and keep the main logic at the top. And it can see the enclosing method's parameters and variables, which is why ValidateInput can use number without it being passed in.

docs.title: Local function versus lambda
docs.text:
Local function Lambda Allocates an object? No, unless it captures Yes — a delegate, plus a closure if it captures Can be recursive? Yes, naturally Awkward Can be called before declaration? Yes No Can be passed as an argument? Yes, converts to a delegate Yes, that is the point Can use yield return? Yes No

Prefer a local function for a private helper. It is faster (often no allocation at all, because the compiler can make it a plain static method), it reads better, and it supports recursion and iterators.

Use a lambda when you are passing behaviour to something — a LINQ operator, an event handler, a callback parameter.

docs.title: The static local function
docs.text:
Adding static stops the function capturing anything from the enclosing method:

public int Process(int[] data)
{
    var multiplier = 3;

    return data.Sum(x => Transform(x));

    static int Transform(int value) => value * 2;
    // 'static' means this CANNOT touch 'multiplier'.
    // Try it and the compiler stops you.
}

Why bother? Because capturing allocates a hidden object (see 1.13). Marking it static guarantees that does not happen, and turns an accidental capture into a compile error instead of a silent allocation.

It is worth making static your default for local functions and only removing it when you genuinely need to capture something.

docs.title: A common real use — separating validation from an iterator
docs.text:
This is a genuinely useful pattern that surprises people:

public IEnumerable<Order> GetOrders(Guid customerId)
{
    if (customerId == Guid.Empty)
        throw new ArgumentException("Invalid id", nameof(customerId));

    return Iterate();

    IEnumerable<Order> Iterate()
    {
        foreach (var order in _db.Orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == customerId))
            yield return order;
    }
}

Why split it? Because a method containing yield return does not run at all until someone enumerates it. So if the validation were in the same method, this would happen:

var orders = GetOrders(Guid.Empty);   // no exception here!
foreach (var o in orders) { }         // exception thrown HERE, far from the cause

Moving the validation into an outer non-iterator method makes it run immediately, so the error appears at the call site where it makes sense. See 2.4.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is a partial class and why does it exist?

It lets one class be split across several files, which the compiler joins back together. Its real purpose is code generation — it allows a tool to own one file while you own another, so regenerating does not overwrite your work. Razor Pages code-behind, EF Core scaffolding, Blazor components and source generators all rely on it. It is not intended as a way to break up a class that has grown too large; if a class needs several files to hold it, the real problem is that the class is doing too much.

Q: What is a partial method?

A method declared in one part of a partial class and optionally implemented in another. If nobody implements it, the compiler removes both the declaration and every call to it, so it costs nothing at runtime. That makes it a zero-cost extension point for generated code — the generator writes a hook, and you implement it only if you need to. Since C# 9 they can return values and be public, but then an implementation is required, because the compiler cannot delete a call whose result is being used.

Q: When would you use a local function instead of a lambda?

For a private helper used only inside one method. A local function is usually cheaper — if it does not capture anything the compiler can emit it as a plain static method with no allocation at all, whereas a lambda always allocates a delegate. It can also be recursive naturally, it can use yield return, and it can be called before it is declared, so you can keep helpers at the bottom of the method. I would use a lambda when I am passing behaviour to something else, like a LINQ operator.

Q: What does static on a local function do?

It prevents the function from capturing variables from the enclosing method. That guarantees no closure object is allocated, and it makes an accidental capture a compile error rather than a silent performance cost. It also documents that the function depends only on its own parameters. It is a good default.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Using partial to hide an oversized class. Splitting it across files makes it harder to see the problem, not easier.
  • A partial method with no implementation is silently removed. Convenient by design, confusing if you did not know and are wondering why your hook never fires.
  • All parts must be in the same assembly and namespace. You cannot split a class across projects.
  • Local functions capture just like lambdas. They are not automatically free — mark them static if you want that guaranteed.
  • A method containing yield return does not execute until enumerated. Argument validation in such a method is delayed. Split it into an outer method plus a local iterator function.
  • Local functions cannot be async void, which is a good thing.

docs.title: 1.25 — Span<T>, Memory<T>, stackalloc
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.24 Partial classes and local functions · Next: 1.26 Modern C# by version

Markers: 🧠 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A Span<T> is a window onto memory you already have. Slicing one costs nothing — no copy, no allocation.
  • Span<T> can only live on the stack. That means you cannot use it in an async method, store it in a field, or put it in a list.
  • Memory<T> is the version that can live on the heap. Use it when you need async.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Imagine you have a 10,000-character string and you want characters 500 to 600.

Substring(500, 100) gives you a new string — which means allocating memory and copying 100 characters into it. If you do that in a loop, you create a lot of garbage.

Span<T> gives you a different option: a window.

Think of a long strip of paper with writing on it, and a piece of card with a rectangular hole cut in it. Put the card over the paper and you can see just the part you want. You did not copy anything. You did not cut the paper. You just narrowed what you are looking at, and you can slide the card along for free.

That is a span. It holds a pointer to where the data starts and how long the window is. Nothing else.

string text = "Hello, World!";

var copy  = text.Substring(7, 5);        // "World" — allocates a new string
var slice = text.AsSpan(7, 5);           // "World" — allocates NOTHING

Both give you "World". Only one of them costs memory.

docs.title: Slicing is free
docs.text:
Span<int> numbers = new int[1000];

var firstHalf  = numbers[..500];       // no allocation
var secondHalf = numbers[500..];       // no allocation
var middle     = numbers.Slice(250, 500);  // no allocation

Each of these is just a new pointer-and-length pair. It is a handful of bytes on the stack, and creating one is essentially free.

A span is a view, not a copy — so writing through it changes the original:

Span<int> data = new int[] { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };
Span<int> part = data[1..3];

part[0] = 99;

Console.WriteLine(data[1]);   // 99 — we changed the original array

docs.title: ReadOnlySpan<T>
docs.text:
The read-only version. string.AsSpan() gives you a ReadOnlySpan<char>, because strings cannot be changed (1.3).

ReadOnlySpan<char> span = "Hello, World!".AsSpan();
ReadOnlySpan<char> word = span[7..12];      // "World", no allocation

docs.title: The restrictions — and why they exist
docs.text:
Span<T> is a ref struct. That is a special kind of struct that the compiler guarantees will only ever live on the stack, never on the heap.

That guarantee is what makes it safe. A span points directly at memory. If a span could outlive the thing it points at, you would have a pointer to memory that has been freed or moved — exactly the class of bug that managed languages exist to prevent.

So the compiler enforces these rules:

class MyClass
{
    private Span<int> _span;         // ERROR — fields live on the heap
}

async Task DoWork()
{
    Span<int> span = stackalloc int[10];
    await Task.Delay(1);             // ERROR — span cannot cross an await
}

var list = new List<Span<int>>();    // ERROR — list contents live on the heap

Span<int> Get() => stackalloc int[10];   // ERROR — the stack memory is gone on return

The async one is the restriction you will hit most often. When a method awaits, all its local variables get moved into a heap object so they survive the pause. A span cannot go on the heap, so it cannot survive an await.

docs.title: Memory<T> — the heap-friendly version
docs.text:
Memory<T> is a normal struct, so it can live on the heap. That means it works in async methods, can be stored in fields, and can be put in collections.

async Task ProcessAsync(Memory<byte> buffer, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await stream.ReadAsync(buffer, ct);       // fine — Memory survives the await

    Span<byte> span = buffer.Span;            // convert when you need to work with it
    ProcessSynchronously(span);
}

The pattern: use Memory<T> for the parts that cross an await, and call .Span to get a Span<T> for the tight synchronous work in between.

Memory<T> is slightly slower than Span<T> because it stores an object reference plus an offset rather than a direct pointer, so every access has a small extra step.

docs.title: stackalloc
docs.text:
Allocates an array directly on the stack instead of the heap:

Span<byte> buffer = stackalloc byte[128];

No heap allocation and no garbage collection — the memory is reclaimed automatically when the method returns.

But the stack is small — usually about 1 MB per thread. Allocate too much and you get a StackOverflowException, which cannot be caught and kills the process immediately.

So the rules are strict:

  • Keep it small. A few hundred bytes to a couple of kilobytes.
  • Never inside a loop — each iteration adds more and none is released until the method returns.
  • Never with a size that comes from user input.

The safe pattern is to check the size and fall back to a pooled array:

const int MaxStack = 256;

Span<byte> buffer = length <= MaxStack
    ? stackalloc byte[MaxStack]
    : new byte[length];

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic parser, showing the difference clearly.

// BEFORE — allocates a string for every field on every line
public static Order ParseLine(string line)
{
    var parts = line.Split(',');        // allocates: array + one string per part
    return new Order
    {
        Id       = Guid.Parse(parts[0]),
        Customer = parts[1],
        Total    = decimal.Parse(parts[2])
    };
}

For a million-line file, that is millions of temporary strings, all of which the garbage collector has to clean up.

// AFTER — no allocation for parsing, only for what we actually keep
public static Order ParseLine(ReadOnlySpan<char> line)
{
    var i1 = line.IndexOf(',');
    var idSpan = line[..i1];

    var rest = line[(i1 + 1)..];
    var i2 = rest.IndexOf(',');
    var customerSpan = rest[..i2];
    var totalSpan = rest[(i2 + 1)..];

    return new Order
    {
        Id       = Guid.Parse(idSpan),          // parses directly from the span
        Customer = customerSpan.ToString(),      // only allocate what we keep
        Total    = decimal.Parse(totalSpan)
    };
}

The key detail: Guid.Parse and decimal.Parse have overloads that take a ReadOnlySpan<char> directly. Most .NET parsing APIs do now. So you never create the intermediate strings at all — you only allocate the one string you actually store.

docs.title: Should you use this everywhere?
docs.text:
No. This code is harder to read than Split, and in most application code that readability cost is not worth it.

Span<T> belongs in:

  • Parsers and serializers processing large volumes
  • Hot loops that show up in a profiler
  • Library code where you do not know how often you will be called

For a controller action that runs a few hundred times a second, Split is completely fine. Measure before you reach for this. Being able to say that in an interview is as valuable as knowing the feature exists.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is Span<T> and what problem does it solve?

It is a view over a contiguous block of memory — an array, a string, or stack-allocated memory. It holds a pointer and a length and nothing else, so creating one or slicing one costs nothing. The problem it solves is the allocations you get from operations like Substring and Split, which copy data into new objects. With a span you can work on part of existing data without copying it, which removes a lot of garbage collection pressure in parsing and serialization code.

Q: Why can't you use Span<T> in an async method?

Because it is a ref struct, which the compiler guarantees will only ever live on the stack. When a method awaits, its local variables have to be moved into a heap object so they survive the suspension — and a span cannot go on the heap. That restriction is what makes spans safe: it guarantees the span can never outlive the memory it points at. When you need something span-like across an await, you use Memory<T>, which is a normal struct and can live on the heap, then convert to a span with .Span for the synchronous work.

Q: What is stackalloc and what should you be careful about?

It allocates an array on the stack rather than the heap, so there is no allocation and no garbage collection — the memory disappears when the method returns. The danger is that the stack is small, typically around a megabyte per thread, and overflowing it throws a StackOverflowException that cannot be caught and kills the process. So you keep it to a few hundred bytes, never put it in a loop, and never size it from user input. The usual pattern is to stack-allocate below a fixed threshold and fall back to a heap or pooled array above it.

Q: When should you actually use spans?

When a profiler tells you allocations are a problem — typically parsers, serializers, and hot loops handling large volumes of data. Span-based code is noticeably harder to read than the equivalent using Substring and Split, so in normal application code that trade is not worth making. It is much more at home in library code, where you do not control how often you are called.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Span<T> cannot be a field, cannot be used in async methods, and cannot go in a collection. All because it is stack-only.
  • stackalloc in a loop will overflow the stack. Each iteration adds more; nothing is released until the method returns.
  • A StackOverflowException cannot be caught. The process dies immediately.
  • A span is a view, not a copy. Writing through it changes the original data, which is surprising if you expected Substring behaviour.
  • Memory<T> is slower than Span<T>. It stores an object reference plus an offset, so each access has an extra indirection.
  • Do not reach for this without measuring. The readability cost is real and the benefit only shows up at volume.
  • A span over an array can be invalidated if the array is resized elsewhere. Do not hold one longer than the immediate operation.

docs.title: 1.26 — Modern C# by Version (C# 8 → 14)
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.25 Span and Memory · Next: 2.1 Collection interfaces

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• The C# version is tied to the .NET version. C# 12 came with .NET 8, C# 13 with .NET 9, C# 14 with .NET 10.
  • The features that changed how everyday code looks: nullable reference types (8), records (9), top-level statements and file-scoped namespaces (10), required members (11), primary constructors and collection expressions (12).
  • In an interview, do not recite the list. Name two or three you have actually used and say what problem they solved.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Interviewers ask "what's new in C#?" for one reason: to find out whether you keep up.

They are not testing whether you can recite a changelog. A candidate who names twelve features they have never used sounds worse than one who names two and explains why they mattered.

So the goal of this note is not to memorise everything. It is to recognise these features when you see them, and to have two or three you can talk about properly.

docs.title: C# 8 (.NET Core 3.0, 2019)
docs.text:
• Nullable reference types — string? and the warnings that go with it. The biggest change to how C# code is written. See 1.15.
  • using declarations — no braces needed. See 1.21.
  • Switch expressions — the => arm form. See 1.17.
  • Default interface methods — see 1.8.
  • IAsyncEnumerable<T> and await foreach — see 2.17.
  • Ranges and indices — array[1..^1], array[^1] for the last element.

docs.title: C# 9 (.NET 5, 2020)
docs.text:
• Records — value equality and with for free. See 1.2.
  • init accessors — immutable properties that still work with object initialisers.
  • Top-level statements — Program.cs without a class or a Main method.
  • Pattern matching improvements — and, or, not, and relational patterns.
  • static lambdas — compiler-enforced "captures nothing". See 1.13.

docs.title: C# 10 (.NET 6, 2021)
docs.text:
• File-scoped namespaces — one less level of indentation everywhere: 
    namespace MyApp.Orders;      // instead of namespace MyApp.Orders { ... }
  • Global usings — declare a using once for the entire project: 
    global using System.Text.Json;
    Combined with <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>, this is why modern files have almost no using lines at the top.
  • record struct — a value-type record. See 1.2.
  • Constant interpolated strings, and improved lambda type inference.

docs.title: C# 11 (.NET 7, 2022)
docs.text:
• required members — the compiler forces the caller to set them. See 1.6.
  • Raw string literals — no more escaping in JSON or SQL: 
    var json = """
    { "name": "Ada", "path": "C:\Users" }
    """;
  • List patterns — if (arr is [1, 2, ..]). See 1.17.
  • Generic maths / static abstract interface members — lets you write T Add<T>(T a, T b) where T supports +.

docs.title: C# 12 (.NET 8, 2023)
docs.text:
• Primary constructors on classes — the biggest everyday change since records: 
    // Before
public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repo;
    private readonly ILogger<OrderService> _logger;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repo, ILogger<OrderService> logger)
    {
        _repo = repo;
        _logger = logger;
    }
}

// After — identical behaviour
public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repo, ILogger<OrderService> logger)
{
    // use 'repo' and 'logger' directly anywhere in the class
}
    This removes a huge amount of boilerplate from every DI-injected service, which is most classes in an ASP.NET Core app.

One caveat worth knowing: unlike a record's primary constructor, a class primary constructor parameter is not a property. It is a private field the compiler creates. It is also mutable, so it is not quite the same as readonly.

  • Collection expressions — one syntax for every collection type: 
    int[] a = [1, 2, 3];
List<int> b = [1, 2, 3];
Span<int> c = [1, 2, 3];
int[] combined = [..a, ..b, 7];      // the spread operator
  • Alias any type — using Point = (int X, int Y);

docs.title: C# 13 (.NET 9, 2024)
docs.text:
• params collections — params now works with Span<T>, List<T> and others, not just arrays. That removes an allocation in common APIs like logging.
  • field keyword (preview) — access the compiler-generated backing field in a property accessor without declaring one.
  • New lock type — System.Threading.Lock, faster than locking on an object.
  • ref and unsafe allowed in more places, including iterators and async methods.

docs.title: C# 14 (.NET 10, 2025)
docs.text:
Ships with .NET 10, the current LTS. Check Microsoft Learn for the confirmed feature list before an interview — this is the version most likely to be probed and the one where a stale memory shows most.

Themes to expect: the field keyword going stable, extension members beyond methods, and further null-safety improvements.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The same class written the old way and the modern way, which is a good thing to be able to show:

// C# 7 style
using System;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;

namespace MyApp.Orders
{
    public class OrderService
    {
        private readonly IOrderRepository _repo;
        private readonly ILogger<OrderService> _logger;

        public OrderService(IOrderRepository repo, ILogger<OrderService> logger)
        {
            _repo = repo ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(repo));
            _logger = logger ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(logger));
        }

        public async Task<OrderDto> GetAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
        {
            var order = await _repo.GetAsync(id, ct);
            if (order == null) throw new NotFoundException(id);

            return new OrderDto
            {
                Id = order.Id,
                Total = order.Total
            };
        }
    }
}

// C# 12 style — same behaviour
namespace MyApp.Orders;                          // file-scoped namespace (C# 10)
                                                 // usings are global (C# 10)
public class OrderService(                       // primary constructor (C# 12)
    IOrderRepository repo,
    ILogger<OrderService> logger)
{
    public async Task<OrderDto> GetAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await repo.GetAsync(id, ct)
                    ?? throw new NotFoundException(id);   // ?? throw (C# 7)

        return new OrderDto { Id = order.Id, Total = order.Total };
    }
}

public record OrderDto                           // record (C# 9)
{
    public required Guid Id { get; init; }       // required + init (C# 9, 11)
    public required decimal Total { get; init; }
}

Roughly half the lines, and nothing important was lost. The null checks are gone because nullable reference types plus required cover them at compile time instead.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What C# features do you use most from recent versions?

The honest answer is more useful than a long list. Something like: "Primary constructors from C# 12 removed a lot of noise — nearly every service in an ASP.NET Core app is just constructor injection, and that used to be six lines of boilerplate per class. Records from C# 9 replaced most of our DTO classes, since value equality and a readable ToString are exactly what you want for a data carrier. And nullable reference types changed how we think about null — turning it on across an existing codebase found several real bugs."

That is three features, each with a reason. It shows use rather than reading.

Q: What is a primary constructor and how does it differ from a record's?

Since C# 12 a class can declare constructor parameters next to its name, and those parameters are usable anywhere in the class body. It removes the field-declare-then-assign boilerplate that every dependency-injected service used to have. The difference from a record is important: a record's primary constructor parameters become public init-only properties with value equality generated around them. A class's primary constructor parameters are just private captured fields — they are not properties, they are not exposed, and they are mutable rather than readonly.

Q: What are collection expressions?

C# 12 introduced [1, 2, 3] as a single syntax that works for arrays, List<T>, Span<T> and any collection type that opts in. It also brought the spread operator, so [..first, ..second, extra] combines collections in one expression. The benefit beyond brevity is that the compiler can pick the most efficient way to build the target type, rather than you having to know which constructor or method is fastest.

Q: How do global usings and implicit usings work?

A global using declares a namespace import once for the whole project rather than per file. Implicit usings, controlled by <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings> in the project file, make the SDK add a standard set automatically based on project type — so a web project gets the common ASP.NET Core namespaces for free. Together they are why a modern file often starts directly with the namespace declaration and no using block at all.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Class primary constructor parameters are not properties. They are private, mutable captured fields. Record primary constructor parameters are public init-only properties. Mixing the two up is a common misunderstanding.
  • Reciting a changelog sounds worse than naming two features you have used.
  • The C# version is tied to the target framework, not chosen freely. You cannot use C# 12 features while targeting .NET 6 without an unsupported override.
  • Global usings can cause name collisions that are hard to trace, because the offending using is not in the file you are looking at.
  • Nullable reference types on an existing project produces hundreds of warnings. Enable it gradually per file with #nullable enable.
  • Do not claim experience with a version you have not used. A single follow-up question will expose it, and calibration matters more than coverage.

docs.title: 2.1 — IEnumerable vs ICollection vs IList vs IQueryable
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 1.26 Modern C# by version · Next: 2.2 Collections and Big-O

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• They form a ladder. Each one adds abilities to the one below it: IEnumerable → ICollection → IList.
  • IEnumerable<T> only lets you walk forward through items, one at a time. That is all.
  • IQueryable<T> is the odd one out. It looks like IEnumerable but it builds a database query instead of looping in memory. Confusing the two is the single most expensive mistake in this topic.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Think of these as job descriptions for a collection. Each one says "here is what you are allowed to do with me".

You pick the smallest one that does the job. If your method only needs to loop through items, ask for IEnumerable<T>. Asking for List<T> when you only loop means callers have to give you a real list — they cannot hand you the results of a database query or a lazily generated sequence.

There is one important twist. Three of these four are about collections in memory. The fourth, IQueryable<T>, is about a query that has not run yet — usually against a database. It shares the same shape but does something completely different underneath, and that difference costs real money in real applications.

docs.title: The ladder
docs.text:
IEnumerable<T>    // walk forward through items. That is it.
    ↓ adds
ICollection<T>    // + Count, Add, Remove, Clear, Contains
    ↓ adds
IList<T>          // + access by position: list[0], Insert, IndexOf

Each level can do everything the level above it can, plus more.

IEnumerable<T> — the smallest. One job: give me items one at a time.

public interface IEnumerable<out T>
{
    IEnumerator<T> GetEnumerator();     // that is the whole interface
}

That single method is what makes foreach work. Notice there is no Count, no Add, no indexing. You cannot ask "how many?" without walking the whole thing.

IEnumerable<Order> orders = GetOrders();

foreach (var o in orders) { }     // allowed
var n = orders.Count();           // allowed, but this is a LINQ method
                                  // that WALKS EVERYTHING to count
var first = orders[0];            // NOT allowed — no indexer
orders.Add(newOrder);             // NOT allowed — read-only

ICollection<T> — adds size and modification.

ICollection<Order> orders = new List<Order>();

orders.Count;              // a real property — instant, no walking
orders.Add(newOrder);
orders.Remove(oldOrder);
orders.Contains(someOrder);
orders.Clear();

orders[0];                 // still NOT allowed — no position access

IList<T> — adds position.

IList<Order> orders = new List<Order>();

orders[0];                 // now allowed
orders.Insert(2, order);
orders.IndexOf(order);

The read-only versions — IReadOnlyCollection<T> and IReadOnlyList<T> — do the same but with no Add or Remove. Use these when returning data you do not want callers changing. See the Code section.

docs.title: The one that is different: IQueryable<T>
docs.text:
IQueryable<T> inherits from IEnumerable<T>, so it looks interchangeable. It is not.

What happens when you call .Where(...) IEnumerable<T> Loops through the items in memory and tests each one with your C# code IQueryable<T> Builds up a description of the query. Nothing runs yet. When you finally ask for results, it is translated into SQL and sent to the database

Here is why that matters enormously:

// IQueryable — the filter is TRANSLATED INTO SQL
IQueryable<Order> query = db.Orders;
var big = query.Where(o => o.Total > 1000).ToList();
// SQL sent: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Total > 1000
// The database does the filtering. Maybe 12 rows come back.

// IEnumerable — the filter happens in YOUR APPLICATION
IEnumerable<Order> all = db.Orders.ToList();     // ← ToList() runs the query NOW
var big = all.Where(o => o.Total > 1000).ToList();
// SQL sent: SELECT * FROM Orders
// ALL ten million rows travel across the network,
// then C# throws away the ones you did not want.

Same-looking code. One returns 12 rows, the other downloads your entire table.

And the trap is how easy it is to do by accident. This method signature causes it:

public IEnumerable<Order> GetOrders() => db.Orders;
//     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ declaring the return as IEnumerable
//     silently turns off SQL translation for every caller

The moment the return type is IEnumerable<T>, any .Where() a caller adds runs in memory, not in the database. Nothing warns you. The code works — it is just catastrophically slower as data grows.

More on this in 2.7 and 13.10.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Rule of thumb: accept the smallest, return the most useful.

// PARAMETERS — ask for the least you need.
// IEnumerable accepts a List, an array, a HashSet, a LINQ result, anything.
public decimal CalculateTotal(IEnumerable<OrderLine> lines)
    => lines.Sum(l => l.Price * l.Quantity);

// If you need the count or to loop more than once, ask for IReadOnlyCollection.
// This signature DOCUMENTS that you will enumerate more than once.
public string Summarise(IReadOnlyCollection<Order> orders)
    => $"{orders.Count} orders, {orders.Sum(o => o.Total):C} total";

// RETURN TYPES — return something concrete enough to be useful,
// but not something callers can modify by accident.
public IReadOnlyList<OrderDto> GetRecent()
{
    return _db.Orders
        .Where(o => o.CreatedAt > DateTime.UtcNow.AddDays(-7))   // runs as SQL
        .Select(o => new OrderDto(o.Id, o.Total))
        .ToList();     // execute HERE, inside the method that owns the DbContext
}

Two deliberate choices in that method, both worth explaining in an interview:

  • .ToList() before returning. The query runs while the DbContext is still alive. If you returned the IQueryable instead, the caller might enumerate it after the context has been disposed at the end of the request — which throws.
  • IReadOnlyList<T> not List<T>. Callers can index and count it, but cannot Add to the collection you handed back. It states that this is a snapshot, not a live list.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between IEnumerable and IList?

They are two rungs of the same ladder. IEnumerable<T> is the smallest possible contract — it only lets you walk forward through the items one at a time, which is what foreach needs. It has no Count, no indexer, and no way to add or remove. IList<T> builds on it through ICollection<T>, adding Count, Add, Remove, and access by position. As a rule I take IEnumerable<T> as a parameter so callers can pass anything, and only ask for something bigger when I genuinely need to count items or index into them.

Q: What is the difference between IEnumerable and IQueryable?

This is the important one. IEnumerable<T> does its work in memory using your compiled C# code — calling Where on it loops through objects and tests each one. IQueryable<T> instead builds up a description of the query as an expression tree, and when you finally ask for the results, a provider like EF Core translates that into SQL and the database does the work. So with IQueryable your filter becomes a WHERE clause, and with IEnumerable the whole table is pulled across the network first and filtered afterwards.

Q: What goes wrong if you return IEnumerable<T> from a repository method?

You silently lose SQL translation. The moment the type is IEnumerable<T>, any Where or OrderBy a caller adds runs in memory rather than in the database — so the query becomes SELECT * over the whole table and the filtering happens after everything has already been transferred. Nothing errors and it works fine on a test database with fifty rows, which is why it usually reaches production before anyone notices. My preference is to execute inside the repository with ToList() and return IReadOnlyList<T>, so nobody can accidentally compose onto a query that has already left its context.

Q: When would you return IReadOnlyList<T> instead of List<T>?

Almost always, for anything crossing a boundary. Returning List<T> hands the caller a live, mutable reference to your data — they can add or remove items and, if you cached that list, you have just let them corrupt your cache. IReadOnlyList<T> still gives them counting and indexing but no mutation, and it communicates that they are looking at a snapshot.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Returning IEnumerable<T> from a data access method kills SQL translation. Filters then run in memory over the full table.
  • .Count() on an IEnumerable walks the entire sequence. .Count on an ICollection is an instant property. The one-character difference matters.
  • Enumerating an IEnumerable twice may run the work twice. For a database query that is two round trips. See 2.6.
  • IReadOnlyList<T> is not a security guarantee. A caller can cast back to List<T>. It communicates intent; it does not enforce it. Use ImmutableList<T> if you need real enforcement.
  • Returning an IQueryable out of a repository leaks the database into your business logic — and it can be enumerated after the DbContext is disposed.
  • IEnumerable<T> is covariant (out T), IList<T> is not. So IEnumerable<Dog> works where IEnumerable<Animal> is expected, but IList<Dog> does not. See 1.10.

docs.title: 2.2 — Core Collections and their Big-O
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.1 Collection interfaces · Next: 2.3 Concurrent collections

Markers: ⭐ 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• List<T> for ordered items you loop through. Dictionary<K,V> for looking things up by a key. HashSet<T> for "have I seen this before?".
  • The big one: searching a List gets slower as it grows; searching a Dictionary or HashSet does not.
  • Picking List where you needed Dictionary is the classic cause of code that is fine in testing and unusable in production.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
First, what does Big-O mean? It is shorthand for "how does this get slower as the collection grows?"

  • O(1) — constant. Same speed with 10 items or 10 million. It jumps straight to the answer.
  • O(n) — linear. Twice the items, twice the time. It has to look at everything.
  • O(log n) — logarithmic. Grows very slowly. Doubling the items adds one extra step.

A useful picture for the two main types:

A List<T> is like a row of numbered lockers. If you know the locker number, you open it instantly — that is O(1). But if you only know what is inside and want to find which locker it is in, you have to open them one by one — O(n).

A Dictionary<K,V> is like a coat check. You hand over a ticket and get your coat back immediately, no searching, however many coats there are. That is O(1) lookup by key, and it is the reason dictionaries exist.

docs.title: The table worth memorising 🎯
docs.text:
Type Add Remove Find by value Find by key/index Keeps order? List<T> O(1)* O(n) O(n) O(1) by index ✅ insertion order Dictionary<K,V> O(1)* O(1) O(n) O(1) by key ❌ no guarantee HashSet<T> O(1)* O(1) O(1) — ❌ no guarantee Queue<T> O(1) O(1) O(n) — ✅ first in, first out Stack<T> O(1) O(1) O(n) — ✅ last in, first out SortedDictionary<K,V> O(log n) O(log n) O(n) O(log n) ✅ sorted by key LinkedList<T> O(1) O(1)** O(n) O(n) ✅ insertion order

* Amortised — meaning "on average". Occasionally the collection is full and has to allocate a bigger internal array and copy everything across, which is O(n). Spread over many adds, the average stays O(1).

** O(1) only if you already hold the node. Finding it first is O(n).

docs.title: List<T> — the default
docs.text:
An array underneath that grows when needed.

var list = new List<Order>();
list.Add(order);           // O(1) — usually just writes to the next slot
list[5];                   // O(1) — jump straight to position 5
list.Contains(order);      // O(n) — checks every item until it finds a match
list.Remove(order);        // O(n) — find it, then shift everything after it down

Performance tip worth knowing: if you know roughly how many items you will add, say so up front:

var list = new List<Order>(capacity: 10_000);
// Without this, the list starts at 4 and doubles: 4, 8, 16, 32...
// Reaching 10,000 means ~11 reallocations and ~20,000 copied references.

docs.title: Dictionary<K,V> — lookup by key
docs.text:
Uses hashing: it runs the key through a function that produces a number, and uses that number to jump straight to the right storage slot. No searching involved — that is why it is O(1).

var byId = new Dictionary<Guid, Order>();
byId[order.Id] = order;              // O(1)
var found = byId[someId];            // O(1) — throws if the key is missing

if (byId.TryGetValue(someId, out var o))    // O(1), no exception if missing
    Console.WriteLine(o.Total);

Use TryGetValue, not ContainsKey followed by an index. The second one hashes the key twice for no reason:

if (byId.ContainsKey(id))     // hashes the key
    var x = byId[id];         // hashes it AGAIN

byId.TryGetValue(id, out var x);   // one lookup, does both

docs.title: HashSet<T> — "have I seen this?"
docs.text:
Same hashing idea, but it stores only values and each one only once.

var seen = new HashSet<string>();
seen.Add("a");           // returns true — it was new
seen.Add("a");           // returns false — already there. No duplicate stored.
seen.Contains("a");      // O(1)

This is the fix for a very common slow pattern:

// SLOW: O(n × m). For 10,000 orders against 10,000 blocked IDs
// that is 100 MILLION comparisons.
var blocked = new List<Guid> { /* 10,000 ids */ };
var flagged = orders.Where(o => blocked.Contains(o.CustomerId)).ToList();

// FAST: O(n). Each Contains is now instant.
var blocked = new HashSet<Guid> { /* 10,000 ids */ };
var flagged = orders.Where(o => blocked.Contains(o.CustomerId)).ToList();

One character changed. Roughly ten-thousand-fold speed difference. This exact fix comes up constantly in real code review, which is why interviewers like the question.

docs.title: Queue<T> and Stack<T>
docs.text:
var queue = new Queue<Job>();     // FIFO — first in, first out. Like a checkout queue.
queue.Enqueue(job);
var next = queue.Dequeue();       // the OLDEST item

var stack = new Stack<Page>();    // LIFO — last in, first out. Like a pile of plates.
stack.Push(page);
var last = stack.Pop();           // the NEWEST item

Use Queue for processing in arrival order, Stack for undo history or backtracking.

docs.title: Choosing — the decision path 🎯
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["What do I need to do most often?"] --> B{"Look items up<br/>by a key?"}
    B -->|Yes| C["Dictionary<K,V>"]
    B -->|No| D{"Just check if<br/>something exists?"}
    D -->|Yes| E["HashSet<T>"]
    D -->|No| F{"Process in a<br/>strict order?"}
    F -->|"Oldest first"| G["Queue<T>"]
    F -->|"Newest first"| H["Stack<T>"]
    F -->|No| I["List<T>"]

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic before-and-after, the kind of thing that turns up in a code review:

// BEFORE — looks harmless, and is fine with 50 customers.
// With 50,000 it takes minutes.
public List<Order> FindVipOrders(List<Order> orders, List<Guid> vipCustomerIds)
{
    var result = new List<Order>();
    foreach (var order in orders)
    {
        if (vipCustomerIds.Contains(order.CustomerId))    // O(n) EVERY time
            result.Add(order);
    }
    return result;
}

Trace the cost: for each of the orders, Contains walks the whole VIP list. So 50,000 orders × 50,000 VIPs = 2.5 billion comparisons.

// AFTER — build the lookup once, then every check is instant.
public List<Order> FindVipOrders(List<Order> orders, IEnumerable<Guid> vipCustomerIds)
{
    var vips = vipCustomerIds.ToHashSet();       // O(n) once, up front

    return orders
        .Where(o => vips.Contains(o.CustomerId)) // O(1) per check
        .ToList();
}

Now it is 50,000 + 50,000 = 100,000 operations instead of 2.5 billion.

The general rule: if you find yourself calling Contains on a List inside a loop, convert it to a HashSet before the loop.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: When would you use a Dictionary instead of a List?

Whenever the main thing I do is look items up by some identifier. A List has to walk through items one at a time to find a match, so lookup gets slower as it grows. A Dictionary hashes the key and jumps straight to the right slot, so it stays fast regardless of size. The trade-off is that a dictionary does not guarantee any particular order and it uses more memory, so if I mostly just loop through everything in sequence, a List is the simpler choice.

Q: What is the difference between a List and a HashSet?

A List keeps items in the order you added them, allows duplicates, and finding a specific item means scanning. A HashSet does not keep order, silently ignores duplicates, and can check whether an item exists instantly because it uses hashing. So if I need "have I seen this before?" or want to remove duplicates, HashSet is right. If order matters or I need to index by position, List is right.

Q: You see list.Contains(x) inside a foreach over another list. What's wrong?

That is O(n × m) — for every item in the outer collection it scans the entire inner collection. It looks fine with small test data and becomes unusable in production. The fix is to build a HashSet from the inner list once before the loop, after which each Contains is O(1). It turns quadratic work into linear, which for two lists of ten thousand is the difference between a hundred million comparisons and twenty thousand.

Q: What does "amortised O(1)" mean for List.Add?

List<T> is backed by an array. Most adds just write into the next free slot, which is O(1). But when the array fills up, it allocates a new one at double the size and copies everything over, which is O(n). Because the doubling means that copy happens increasingly rarely, the average cost per add across many adds still works out as constant — that is what "amortised" means. If you know the final size, passing a capacity to the constructor avoids the reallocations entirely.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• List.Contains inside a loop is quadratic. The single most common performance bug in this topic. Use a HashSet.
  • Dictionary and HashSet do not guarantee order. Never rely on the order you get back from iterating one, even if it looks stable in testing.
  • A custom class used as a dictionary key must override Equals and GetHashCode. Without that, two objects with identical contents are treated as different keys and lookups mysteriously fail. Records do this for you — see 1.2.
  • Mutating an object after using it as a key breaks the dictionary. Its hash changes, so it lands in a different slot and can never be found again. Keys should be immutable.
  • dictionary[missingKey] throws. TryGetValue does not. Use it.
  • ContainsKey followed by [key] hashes twice. TryGetValue does it in one pass.
  • None of these are thread-safe. Two threads writing to a Dictionary at once can corrupt it or spin forever. See 2.3.

docs.title: 2.3 — Concurrent Collections
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.2 Collections and Big-O · Next: 2.4 yield and iterators

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• The normal collections (List, Dictionary) are not safe when several threads write to them at once. They can corrupt themselves or hang forever.
  • ConcurrentDictionary<K,V> is the one you will actually use. In ASP.NET Core, every request runs on its own thread, so any shared collection needs this.
  • Thread-safe on each operation is not the same as thread-safe overall. Two safe calls in a row can still race.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
In a web application, many requests are handled at the same time, on different threads. If they all touch the same Dictionary, they are all reaching into the same object at once.

Why is that dangerous? Because operations that look like one step are really several. Adding to a Dictionary might mean: work out the slot, check if it is full, resize the internal array, copy everything across, write the value. If a second thread interrupts halfway through, it sees a half-rebuilt structure.

A picture: two people editing the same paper address book at the same time. One is midway through copying every entry onto a bigger sheet because the old one filled up. The other writes a new entry onto the old sheet. That entry vanishes. Or worse, the book ends up with a page pointing at itself and anyone reading it walks in circles forever.

That last one is real. A corrupted Dictionary in .NET Framework could put a thread into an infinite loop, pinning a CPU core at 100% until the process was restarted.

The System.Collections.Concurrent namespace has replacements that handle this properly.

docs.title: The types
docs.text:
Concurrent type Replaces Use it for ConcurrentDictionary<K,V> Dictionary<K,V> Shared lookups. By far the most used. ConcurrentQueue<T> Queue<T> Work items processed oldest-first ConcurrentStack<T> Stack<T> Work items processed newest-first ConcurrentBag<T> List<T> (unordered) Many threads adding, order irrelevant BlockingCollection<T> — Producer/consumer with a size limit

There is deliberately no ConcurrentList<T>. A list is about position, and positions stop being meaningful when other threads are inserting and removing underneath you. If you need a shared ordered list, either lock around it or use ImmutableList<T>.

docs.title: ConcurrentDictionary — the important one
docs.text:
private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, User> _cache = new();

_cache["key"] = user;                       // safe
_cache.TryGetValue("key", out var found);   // safe
_cache.TryRemove("key", out var removed);   // safe

The methods that make it genuinely useful are the combined ones:

// GetOrAdd — if the key exists return it, otherwise create, store and return it.
// The whole check-and-add is ONE atomic operation.
var user = _cache.GetOrAdd(userId, id => LoadUserFromDatabase(id));

// AddOrUpdate — insert if new, otherwise compute a new value from the old one
_cache.AddOrUpdate(
    key: userId,
    addValue: 1,                        // if not present, store 1
    updateValueFactory: (k, old) => old + 1);   // if present, add 1 to it

Without GetOrAdd, you would write this — and it is broken:

// BROKEN even with a ConcurrentDictionary
if (!_cache.ContainsKey(id))         // thread A: not there
{                                    // thread B: also not there
    _cache[id] = Load(id);           // BOTH load. Both write. Wasted work,
}                                    // and possibly two different objects.

Each individual call is thread-safe. The sequence is not. This is the single most important idea in this note.

docs.title: ⚠️ The factory can run more than once
docs.text:
GetOrAdd is atomic in what it stores — only one value ever wins. But the factory function you pass in is not locked, and can be executed by several threads at the same time:

var user = _cache.GetOrAdd(id, key =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("Loading...");    // this CAN print twice for the same key
    return LoadFromDatabase(key);       // only one result is kept
});

That is a deliberate design choice — holding a lock while running arbitrary user code is how you get deadlocks. But it means:

  • If the factory is expensive, you may pay for it several times.
  • If the factory has side effects (writes a file, sends an email), those happen more than once.

The fix when it matters is to store a Lazy<T>, because Lazy guarantees its factory runs only once:

private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, Lazy<User>> _cache = new();

var user = _cache
    .GetOrAdd(id, key => new Lazy<User>(() => LoadFromDatabase(key)))
    .Value;      // only the winning Lazy is ever evaluated

docs.title: BlockingCollection<T> — producer and consumer
docs.text:
Useful when one part of your code produces work and another consumes it, and you want the producer to slow down if the consumer falls behind:

var queue = new BlockingCollection<Job>(boundedCapacity: 100);

// Producer — blocks if there are already 100 waiting
Task.Run(() =>
{
    foreach (var job in GetJobs())
        queue.Add(job);
    queue.CompleteAdding();      // signals "no more coming"
});

// Consumer — blocks until an item arrives, exits when adding is complete
Task.Run(() =>
{
    foreach (var job in queue.GetConsumingEnumerable())
        Process(job);
});

The capacity limit is the point. Without it, a fast producer builds an unbounded queue in memory until the process runs out.

In modern ASP.NET Core, prefer System.Threading.Channels for this. It does the same job with proper async support, so consumers await instead of blocking a thread. See 21.1.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The realistic ASP.NET Core case — a shared in-memory cache in a singleton service:

public class ExchangeRateService(IHttpClientFactory factory)
{
    // Singleton service, so this dictionary is shared by EVERY request
    // happening at the same time. It MUST be concurrent.
    private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, Lazy<Task<decimal>>> _rates = new();

    public Task<decimal> GetRateAsync(string currency)
    {
        return _rates.GetOrAdd(
            currency,
            key => new Lazy<Task<decimal>>(() => FetchRateAsync(key))
        ).Value;
    }

    private async Task<decimal> FetchRateAsync(string currency)
    {
        var client = factory.CreateClient("rates");
        return await client.GetFromJsonAsync<decimal>($"/rate/{currency}");
    }
}

Why Lazy<Task<decimal>> and not just Task<decimal>? Because without Lazy, fifty simultaneous requests for the same currency could each start their own HTTP call before any of them finished. With Lazy, only one call is ever made and the other forty-nine await the same task. That pattern is called stampede protection — 19.4 covers it properly.

But in a real ASP.NET Core app, reach for IMemoryCache first. It gives you expiry, size limits and eviction, which a raw ConcurrentDictionary does not — a dictionary that only ever grows is a memory leak. See 19.2.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why can't you just use a Dictionary in a multi-threaded application?

Because its operations are not atomic. Adding an item can involve resizing the internal array and copying everything into it, and if another thread reads or writes partway through that, it sees an inconsistent structure. In the worst case the internal links become circular and a reading thread spins forever at 100% CPU. In ASP.NET Core this matters constantly, because requests are handled concurrently on different threads, so anything stored in a singleton is shared across all of them.

Q: What does GetOrAdd do, and what is the catch?

It returns the existing value for a key, or creates one with the factory you supply, stores it and returns that — as a single atomic operation, so you avoid the classic check-then-add race. The catch is that only the storing is atomic. The factory itself is not locked, so several threads can run it simultaneously for the same key even though only one result is kept. If the factory is expensive or has side effects, you wrap the value in a Lazy<T>, because Lazy does guarantee its factory runs once.

Q: Is a ConcurrentDictionary enough to make my code thread-safe?

No, and this is the important distinction. Each individual method on it is thread-safe, but a sequence of calls is not. Writing if (!dict.ContainsKey(k)) dict[k] = value is still racy, because another thread can insert between the check and the write. That is exactly why the combined methods like GetOrAdd and AddOrUpdate exist — they collapse the sequence into one atomic step.

Q: Why is there no ConcurrentList<T>?

Because a list is defined by position, and position is meaningless once other threads can insert and remove concurrently — index 5 could refer to a different item by the time you use it, and an index that was valid when you checked could be out of range a moment later. There is no sensible way to make that safe. If you need shared ordered data, you either lock around a normal list or use an immutable collection where every change produces a new version.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Thread-safe operations do not make thread-safe logic. Check-then-act across two calls is still a race, even on a concurrent collection.
  • The GetOrAdd factory can run several times. Only one result is stored, but the work may be done more than once. Wrap in Lazy<T> if that matters.
  • Concurrent collections are slower for single-threaded use. They pay for synchronisation you are not using. Do not use them "just in case".
  • Count on a concurrent collection is a snapshot and may be stale the instant you read it. Never use it for a decision that must be exact.
  • Enumerating a concurrent collection gives you a moment-in-time view. Items may be added or removed while you loop; you will not see a consistent snapshot.
  • A ConcurrentDictionary that only grows is a memory leak. It has no eviction. Use IMemoryCache for anything cache-shaped.
  • ConcurrentBag is optimised for the same thread adding and removing. If one thread produces and another consumes, ConcurrentQueue is usually faster.
