docs.title: 2.4 — IEnumerator, yield return, Deferred Execution
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.3 Concurrent collections · Next: 2.5 LINQ basics

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• yield return lets you produce items one at a time, on demand, instead of building a whole list first.
  • A method containing yield return does not run at all until someone starts looping over its result. That surprises people.
  • The compiler rewrites the method into a hidden state machine class that remembers where it got to.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Normally a method does all its work and then hands back a finished result. If it returns a thousand items, all thousand exist in memory before the caller sees the first one.

yield return changes that. It lets the method hand back one item, pause, and wait. When the caller asks for the next one, the method resumes exactly where it stopped.

A picture: a vending machine versus a delivery van.

A normal method is the delivery van — it turns up with the entire order at once, and you need somewhere to put all of it. A yield return method is the vending machine — you press the button, one item drops out, and nothing else moves until you press again.

Why does that matter? Two reasons:

  • Memory. Reading a million-line file into a List<string> needs memory for a million strings. Yielding them one at a time needs memory for one.
  • Stopping early. If you only want the first match, the vending machine stops after the first press. The van has already driven the whole route.

docs.title: The basic shape
docs.text:
public IEnumerable<int> GetNumbers()
{
    Console.WriteLine("  starting");
    yield return 1;
    Console.WriteLine("  after 1");
    yield return 2;
    Console.WriteLine("  after 2");
    yield return 3;
}

Now watch the execution order carefully — this is the part that catches people out:

Console.WriteLine("calling the method");
var numbers = GetNumbers();
Console.WriteLine("method returned");

foreach (var n in numbers)
    Console.WriteLine($"got {n}");

Output:

calling the method
method returned          ← the method body has NOT run yet!
  starting
got 1
  after 1
got 2
  after 2
got 3

Notice that "starting" prints after "method returned". Calling the method did nothing at all. The body only began running when foreach asked for the first item.

docs.title: What the compiler actually does
docs.text:
It rewrites your method into a hidden class that implements IEnumerator<T> and remembers a position number. Roughly:

// Compiler-generated, simplified
class Hidden : IEnumerator<int>
{
    int _state = 0;
    public int Current { get; private set; }

    public bool MoveNext()
    {
        switch (_state)
        {
            case 0: Current = 1; _state = 1; return true;   // stop after 'yield return 1'
            case 1: Current = 2; _state = 2; return true;
            case 2: Current = 3; _state = 3; return true;
            default: return false;                          // no more items
        }
    }
}

And foreach is really just this loop:

var e = numbers.GetEnumerator();
while (e.MoveNext())              // "is there another? if so, load it into Current"
{
    var n = e.Current;
}

So yield return is a pause point. Each MoveNext() runs the method until the next yield return, then freezes it again.

docs.title: yield break
docs.text:
Stops the sequence early:

public IEnumerable<int> TakeUntilNegative(IEnumerable<int> source)
{
    foreach (var n in source)
    {
        if (n < 0) yield break;    // stop producing, cleanly
        yield return n;
    }
}

docs.title: The memory win
docs.text:
// Loads the ENTIRE file into memory first
public List<string> ReadAllLines(string path)
{
    var lines = new List<string>();
    foreach (var line in File.ReadLines(path))
        lines.Add(line);
    return lines;
}
// A 2 GB log file needs 2 GB of RAM. Might not even fit.

// Reads one line at a time
public IEnumerable<string> ReadLines(string path)
{
    using var reader = new StreamReader(path);
    string? line;
    while ((line = reader.ReadLine()) is not null)
        yield return line;
}
// A 2 GB file uses memory for ONE line.

And with the second version, stopping early actually stops:

var firstError = ReadLines("huge.log").First(l => l.Contains("ERROR"));
// If the error is on line 3, the file reader closes after line 3.
// The other two gigabytes are never touched.

Note the using inside the iterator. When the caller stops looping — whether normally, by breaking out, or because of an exception — the compiler runs the disposal properly. That is handled for you.

docs.title: ⚠️ The validation trap
docs.text:
This is the one to remember, and it is a genuinely common bug.

public IEnumerable<Order> GetOrders(Guid customerId)
{
    if (customerId == Guid.Empty)
        throw new ArgumentException("Invalid id", nameof(customerId));   // ← never runs on time

    foreach (var order in _db.Orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == customerId))
        yield return order;
}

Because the method contains yield return, the entire body is deferred — including the validation at the top:

var orders = GetOrders(Guid.Empty);   // NO exception here. Nothing ran.

// ... 50 lines of other code ...

foreach (var o in orders) { }          // exception thrown HERE, far from the cause

The stack trace points at the foreach, not at the bad argument. Debugging that is miserable.

The fix: split it into two methods. An outer normal method that validates immediately, and an inner iterator:

public IEnumerable<Order> GetOrders(Guid customerId)
{
    if (customerId == Guid.Empty)
        throw new ArgumentException("Invalid id", nameof(customerId));

    return Iterate();      // this line runs immediately

    IEnumerable<Order> Iterate()      // a local function — see 1.24
    {
        foreach (var order in _db.Orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == customerId))
            yield return order;
    }
}

Now GetOrders is a normal method — no yield in its own body — so its validation runs the moment it is called. Only Iterate is deferred.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic streaming example — processing a large CSV without loading it all:

public IEnumerable<Order> ParseOrders(string path)
{
    if (!File.Exists(path))
        throw new FileNotFoundException(path);      // runs immediately

    return Parse();

    IEnumerable<Order> Parse()
    {
        using var reader = new StreamReader(path);
        reader.ReadLine();                          // skip the header row

        string? line;
        while ((line = reader.ReadLine()) is not null)
        {
            var parts = line.Split(',');
            yield return new Order
            {
                Id       = Guid.Parse(parts[0]),
                Customer = parts[1],
                Total    = decimal.Parse(parts[2])
            };
        }
    }
}

Used with LINQ, the whole pipeline stays lazy:

var firstBigOrder = ParseOrders("orders.csv")
    .Where(o => o.Total > 10_000)
    .FirstOrDefault();

// Reads the file line by line and STOPS at the first match.
// A 5 GB file where the match is on line 12 reads 12 lines.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does yield return do?

It turns a method into an iterator that produces values one at a time instead of building and returning a whole collection. Each yield return hands one item back and pauses the method; when the caller asks for the next item, execution resumes from exactly that point. The compiler implements this by rewriting the method into a hidden class that implements IEnumerator<T> and tracks a state number, so the "pause and resume" is really a switch statement on that state.

Q: When is the body of an iterator method executed?

Not when you call it. Calling it just creates the state machine object and returns immediately. The body only starts running when something calls MoveNext on the enumerator, which in practice means when a foreach begins or when a LINQ operator that forces execution runs. That is why it is called deferred execution, and it is why argument validation inside an iterator method fires at the wrong time.

Q: What is wrong with validating arguments inside an iterator method?

The validation is deferred along with everything else, so it does not throw when the method is called — it throws whenever the caller eventually enumerates the result, which might be much later and in a completely different part of the code. The stack trace then points at the foreach rather than at the bad argument. The fix is to split it: a normal outer method that validates and then returns a local iterator function, so validation runs eagerly and only the iteration is deferred.

Q: What is the benefit of an iterator over just returning a List?

Memory and early exit. A List has to hold everything at once, so reading a two-gigabyte file means two gigabytes of RAM. An iterator holds one item at a time. And because items are produced on demand, an operation like First or Any stops the producer as soon as it has what it needs, so you never do the work of generating the rest. The trade-off is that the sequence can only be walked forward, and walking it twice does the work twice.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• The whole method body is deferred, including validation. Split into an outer validating method plus an inner iterator.
  • Enumerating twice runs the method twice. For a file read or a database query that is two full passes. See 2.6.
  • You cannot use ref or out parameters in an iterator method. The compiler rejects it, because those cannot be stored in the state machine.
  • try/catch around a yield return is not allowed. You can use try/finally, and using works, but you cannot catch around a yield point.
  • Iterators are forward-only. No index, no Count, and no going back.
  • Captured variables are shared with the state machine. If the caller changes a variable the iterator captured, the iterator sees the new value on the next MoveNext.
  • IEnumerable is not thread-safe. Two threads enumerating the same iterator instance will corrupt its state.

docs.title: 2.5 — LINQ: Query vs Method Syntax, and the Standard Operators
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.4 yield and iterators · Next: 2.6 Deferred execution

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• LINQ is a set of extension methods on IEnumerable<T> that filter, transform and combine sequences.
  • Two ways to write it. Method syntax (.Where(x => ...)) is what almost everyone uses. Query syntax (from x in ... where ...) compiles down to exactly the same thing.
  • Operators split into two groups: those that return a new sequence (lazy) and those that return a single value (run immediately).

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Before LINQ, filtering a list meant writing the loop yourself:

var result = new List<Order>();
foreach (var o in orders)
{
    if (o.Total > 100)
        result.Add(o);
}

Five lines that say almost nothing about intent. LINQ replaces it with one that does:

var result = orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100).ToList();

The point is not brevity for its own sake. It is that you describe what you want, not how to loop. That makes the code read like the requirement, and it means the same expression can run in memory or be translated into SQL without you rewriting it — see 2.7.

LINQ stands for Language Integrated Query. Every operator is an extension method (1.14) on IEnumerable<T>, and almost all of them take a delegate (1.11) — usually written as a lambda.

docs.title: The two syntaxes
docs.text:
They are equivalent. The compiler rewrites query syntax into method calls before anything runs.

// Query syntax — looks like SQL
var result = from o in orders
             where o.Total > 100
             orderby o.CreatedAt descending
             select o.CustomerName;

// Method syntax — identical after compilation
var result = orders
    .Where(o => o.Total > 100)
    .OrderByDescending(o => o.CreatedAt)
    .Select(o => o.CustomerName);

Method syntax is the common choice and what you should default to. Query syntax only wins in two cases — joins and multiple let variables — where it genuinely reads better:

// Query syntax is clearly nicer here
var result = from o in orders
             join c in customers on o.CustomerId equals c.Id
             let discount = o.Total * 0.1m
             where discount > 5
             select new { c.Name, o.Total, discount };

The method-syntax equivalent of that join is noticeably uglier. Mixing both in one codebase is fine.

docs.title: The operators worth knowing
docs.text:
Filtering — narrows the sequence

orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100);           // keep matching items
orders.OfType<PriorityOrder>();             // keep items of a given type
orders.Distinct();                          // remove duplicates
orders.DistinctBy(o => o.CustomerId);       // .NET 6+ — distinct by a key
orders.Take(10);                            // first 10
orders.Skip(20).Take(10);                   // paging: items 21-30
orders.TakeWhile(o => o.Total > 0);         // take until the test fails

Projecting — changes the shape

orders.Select(o => o.CustomerName);         // one output per input
orders.Select((o, i) => $"{i}: {o.Id}");    // with the index
orders.SelectMany(o => o.Lines);            // FLATTEN a list of lists

SelectMany is worth pausing on, because people find it confusing. Select gives you a sequence of lists; SelectMany glues them into one:

// orders has 3 orders, each with 4 lines

orders.Select(o => o.Lines);       // IEnumerable<List<OrderLine>> — 3 items
orders.SelectMany(o => o.Lines);   // IEnumerable<OrderLine>       — 12 items

Ordering

orders.OrderBy(o => o.CreatedAt);
orders.OrderByDescending(o => o.Total);
orders.OrderBy(o => o.Status).ThenBy(o => o.Total);   // ThenBy for the tiebreak
orders.Reverse();

⚠️ Use ThenBy for a second sort key, not a second OrderBy. Two OrderBy calls throw the first sort away entirely — the second one re-sorts from scratch.

Aggregating — these return a single value and run immediately

orders.Count();                             // how many
orders.Count(o => o.Total > 100);           // how many match
orders.Sum(o => o.Total);
orders.Average(o => o.Total);
orders.Min(o => o.Total);
orders.MaxBy(o => o.Total);                 // .NET 6+ — the ORDER, not the total
orders.Any();                               // is there at least one?
orders.Any(o => o.Total > 1000);            // does anything match?
orders.All(o => o.Total > 0);               // do they all match?

⚠️ Use Any() rather than Count() > 0. Any() stops at the first item it finds; Count() walks the entire sequence just to throw the number away. Against a database that is EXISTS versus COUNT(*).

Element access — covered properly in 2.9

orders.First();  orders.FirstOrDefault();
orders.Single(); orders.SingleOrDefault();
orders.ElementAt(3);

Set operations

listA.Union(listB);          // everything, no duplicates
listA.Intersect(listB);      // only items in both
listA.Except(listB);         // in A but not in B
listA.Concat(listB);         // everything, duplicates kept
listA.SequenceEqual(listB);  // same items, same order?

Materialising — forces execution and gives you a real collection

orders.ToList();
orders.ToArray();
orders.ToDictionary(o => o.Id);
orders.ToHashSet();
orders.ToLookup(o => o.CustomerId);     // like a dictionary, but many values per key

docs.title: Lazy or immediate?
docs.text:
This split matters more than any individual operator:

Returns a sequence — lazy Returns one value or a collection — runs now Where, Select, SelectMany Count, Sum, Average, Min, Max OrderBy, ThenBy, Reverse First, Single, Last, ElementAt Take, Skip, Distinct Any, All, Contains Union, Intersect, Except, Concat ToList, ToArray, ToDictionary

Nothing in the left column does any work until something from the right column asks for results. That is 2.6, and it is the source of most LINQ surprises.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic pipeline, and how to keep it readable:

public IReadOnlyList<CustomerSummary> BuildSummaries(
    IEnumerable<Order> orders,
    DateTime since)
{
    return orders
        .Where(o => o.CreatedAt >= since)          // narrow FIRST — cheapest step
        .Where(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Complete)
        .GroupBy(o => o.CustomerId)                // one group per customer
        .Select(g => new CustomerSummary
        {
            CustomerId = g.Key,                    // Key is what you grouped by
            OrderCount = g.Count(),                // g is the orders in this group
            TotalSpent = g.Sum(o => o.Total),
            LastOrder  = g.Max(o => o.CreatedAt)
        })
        .OrderByDescending(s => s.TotalSpent)      // sort LAST — fewest items by now
        .Take(100)
        .ToList();                                 // one pass, executed here
}

Two ordering rules that are worth stating in an interview:

  • Filter before you project or sort. Every later step then has less to do. Sorting ten thousand items and then keeping five is wasted work.
  • ToList() exactly once, at the end. Calling it midway forces everything up to that point into memory and throws away the laziness.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between query syntax and method syntax?

Nothing, functionally. The compiler translates query syntax into method calls before anything runs, so both produce identical code. Method syntax is more common because it covers every operator — some, like Count and ToList, have no query-syntax equivalent — and it chains naturally. Query syntax is genuinely nicer for joins and for cases where you need intermediate variables with let. Most codebases use method syntax by default and drop into query syntax for complex joins.

Q: What is the difference between Select and SelectMany?

Select transforms each item into exactly one output, so if each order has a list of lines, Select(o => o.Lines) gives you a sequence of lists. SelectMany does the same transformation but then flattens the results into a single sequence, so you get all the lines together rather than grouped by order. Whenever your projection returns a collection and you want the contents rather than the collections, SelectMany is the one.

Q: Why prefer Any() over Count() > 0?

Any() stops as soon as it finds one item, whereas Count() walks the entire sequence and then compares. On an in-memory list that is a waste; against a database it is the difference between an EXISTS query that can stop at the first row and a COUNT(*) that scans everything. The same reasoning applies to Any(predicate) over Where(predicate).Count() > 0.

Q: Does the order of LINQ operators matter?

Yes, both for correctness and performance. Filtering early means every subsequent operator handles fewer items, so Where before OrderBy is much cheaper than the reverse. Some orderings also change the result — Skip then Take is paging, while Take then Skip is not. And a second OrderBy discards the first sort entirely, which is why you need ThenBy for a secondary key.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• A second OrderBy discards the first sort. Use ThenBy for secondary ordering.
  • Count() > 0 instead of Any() walks the whole sequence for no reason.
  • Calling ToList() in the middle of a chain forces everything into memory and kills laziness. Do it once, at the end.
  • Select when you meant SelectMany leaves you with a sequence of collections.
  • Sum on an empty sequence returns 0, but Average, Min and Max throw. Guard with Any() or use nullable versions.
  • LINQ over an IQueryable has different capabilities to LINQ over objects. Some C# methods have no SQL equivalent and will either throw or silently pull the whole table. See 13.10.
  • OrderBy has to buffer everything to sort it, so it cannot stay fully lazy — it reads the entire source before producing the first item.

docs.title: 2.6 — Deferred vs Immediate Execution
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.5 LINQ basics · Next: 2.7 Expression trees

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A LINQ query is a recipe, not a meal. Writing it does nothing. It only runs when something asks for results.
  • Enumerating it twice runs it twice — two database round trips, two file reads, two of everything.
  • The fix is .ToList() once, at the point you know you need the data.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
This is the single most surprising thing about LINQ, and it causes real production bugs.

When you write this:

var expensive = orders.Where(o => o.Total > 1000);

nothing has happened. No filtering. No looping. expensive is not a list of orders — it is an object that knows how to produce those orders when asked.

The cooking analogy fits well. A recipe card that says "chop onions, fry them, add stock" is not soup. You can carry the card around, hand it to someone, even add steps to it. No cooking happens until someone actually stands at the stove.

And here is the consequence people miss: hand the same recipe to two people and the meal gets cooked twice. LINQ does exactly that. Every time you enumerate a query, the whole thing runs again from the start.

docs.title: Proving it to yourself
docs.text:
var numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 };

var query = numbers.Where(n =>
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  testing {n}");
    return n > 1;
});

Console.WriteLine("query created");
Console.WriteLine("--- first loop ---");
foreach (var n in query) { }
Console.WriteLine("--- second loop ---");
foreach (var n in query) { }

Output:

query created            ← nothing tested yet
--- first loop ---
  testing 1
  testing 2
  testing 3
--- second loop ---
  testing 1              ← it all runs AGAIN
  testing 2
  testing 3

The filter ran six times for three items.

docs.title: The other half: the source can change underneath you
docs.text:
Because the query holds a reference to the source rather than a copy, changing the source changes the results:

var numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 };
var evens = numbers.Where(n => n % 2 == 0);

Console.WriteLine(evens.Count());     // 1  (just the 2)

numbers.Add(4);
numbers.Add(6);

Console.WriteLine(evens.Count());     // 3  — the query saw the new items!

The evens variable was never reassigned, yet its answer changed. That is deferred execution. Sometimes it is exactly what you want; more often it is a bug waiting to happen.

docs.title: What triggers execution
docs.text:
Deferred — builds the recipe Immediate — cooks it Where, Select, SelectMany ToList, ToArray, ToDictionary, ToHashSet OrderBy, ThenBy, Take, Skip Count, Sum, Average, Min, Max Distinct, Concat, Union, Reverse First, Single, Last, ElementAt GroupBy*, Join* Any, All, Contains foreach over it

* GroupBy and Join are technically deferred, but when they do run they have to read the entire source before yielding anything, because they cannot know the groups until they have seen everything.

docs.title: 1. The same database query running several times
docs.text:
// BAD — three separate SQL queries
var orders = _db.Orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == id);

var count = orders.Count();                     // SQL round trip 1
var total = orders.Sum(o => o.Total);           // SQL round trip 2
var list  = orders.ToList();                    // SQL round trip 3

Three trips to the database for data you only needed once. On a busy endpoint that is three times the database load.

// GOOD — one query, then work in memory
var orders = await _db.Orders
    .Where(o => o.CustomerId == id)
    .ToListAsync(ct);                           // SQL round trip 1, and only

var count = orders.Count;                       // now a plain property
var total = orders.Sum(o => o.Total);           // now in-memory

docs.title: 2. Enumerating after the DbContext is gone
docs.text:
public IEnumerable<Order> GetOrders(Guid id)
{
    using var db = new AppDbContext();
    return db.Orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == id);
}       // ← the DbContext is disposed HERE, before anything ran

var orders = GetOrders(id);
foreach (var o in orders) { }
// ObjectDisposedException — "Cannot access a disposed context instance"

The query never ran inside the method. By the time it does, its database connection is gone. Add .ToList() before returning.

docs.title: 3. The captured-variable surprise
docs.text:
var threshold = 100;
var expensive = orders.Where(o => o.Total > threshold);

threshold = 1000;                      // change the variable

var results = expensive.ToList();      // uses 1000, NOT 100

The lambda captured the variable, not its value at the time (1.13). Because execution is deferred, it reads whatever the variable holds at execution time.

docs.title: 4. Exceptions thrown far from their cause
docs.text:
var parsed = lines.Select(l => int.Parse(l));   // no exception yet

// ... 40 lines of unrelated code ...

var sum = parsed.Sum();      // FormatException thrown HERE

The stack trace points at Sum(), which has nothing to do with the malformed input.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The practical rule, applied:

public async Task<OrderReport> BuildReportAsync(Guid customerId, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // Build the query — still just a recipe. Nothing has run.
    var query = _db.Orders
        .Where(o => o.CustomerId == customerId)
        .Where(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Complete);

    // Compose conditionally — still free, still nothing running
    if (_settings.ExcludeRefunds)
        query = query.Where(o => !o.WasRefunded);

    // Execute ONCE, deliberately, while the context is alive
    var orders = await query
        .Select(o => new OrderSummary(o.Id, o.Total, o.CreatedAt))
        .ToListAsync(ct);

    // Everything below works on the in-memory list. No more SQL.
    return new OrderReport
    {
        Count      = orders.Count,
        Total      = orders.Sum(o => o.Total),
        Largest    = orders.MaxBy(o => o.Total),
        FirstOrder = orders.MinBy(o => o.CreatedAt)
    };
}

The pattern to remember:

  1. Compose while it is cheap. Adding Where clauses to an unexecuted query costs nothing and lets you build conditional filters cleanly.
  2. Execute once, on purpose, at the moment you need real data.
  3. After that, you have a list — use it as many times as you like.

docs.title: When deferred execution is a feature
docs.text:
It is not always a hazard. Conditional query building, as above, only works because execution is deferred. So does infinite generation:

static IEnumerable<int> Naturals()
{
    var i = 0;
    while (true) yield return i++;      // never ends
}

var firstTen = Naturals().Take(10).ToList();    // fine — Take stops it

That would be impossible if Naturals() had to finish before Take could run.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is deferred execution in LINQ?

Most LINQ operators do not run when you write them. They return an object that describes the query, and the work only happens when something enumerates it — a foreach, or an operator like ToList, Count or First. So a LINQ statement is a recipe rather than a result. The practical consequence is that enumerating the same query variable twice executes it twice, and that the source data is read at execution time, not at the point the query was written.

Q: What problems does it cause in practice?

Three main ones. Multiple enumeration — calling Count() and then ToList() on the same query means two full executions, which against a database is two round trips. Disposed context — if a method builds a query over a DbContext and returns it without calling ToList, the context is disposed before the query runs and enumeration throws. And late exceptions — a parsing error inside a Select surfaces wherever the query is finally enumerated, so the stack trace points somewhere unrelated to the actual problem.

Q: How do you avoid multiple enumeration?

Call ToList() or ToArray() once, at the point you know you need the data, and use the resulting collection from then on. The signal to watch for is a variable of type IEnumerable<T> being used more than once — most analysers, including ReSharper, flag it as "possible multiple enumeration". The other half is being deliberate about method signatures: returning IEnumerable<T> from a data access method invites the problem, so I return IReadOnlyList<T> after materialising inside.

Q: Is deferred execution ever useful?

Yes, and it is why the design exists. It lets you build a query in pieces — adding Where clauses conditionally based on which filters a user supplied — and only pay for it once, as a single SQL statement. It also allows infinite sequences, because Take(10) can stop an endless generator after ten items. And it means an early-exit operator like First stops the whole pipeline as soon as it has an answer instead of processing everything.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Enumerating a query variable twice executes it twice. Two database round trips, two file reads, two of whatever the source is.
  • Returning an unexecuted query from a method whose DbContext is disposed throws ObjectDisposedException at the caller.
  • Captured variables are read at execution time, not when the query was written.
  • Exceptions surface at the enumeration point, not where the faulty operation was declared.
  • OrderBy and GroupBy buffer the entire source before producing anything, so they are deferred but not streaming.
  • .ToList() in the middle of a chain throws away laziness for everything after it, and materialises more rows than you need.
  • A query over a mutable collection sees later changes. The result can differ between two enumerations even with no code change in between.

docs.title: 2.7 — IQueryable and Expression Trees: How LINQ Becomes SQL
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.6 Deferred execution · Next: 2.8 Advanced LINQ operators

Markers: ⭐ 🧠 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Func<T,bool> is compiled code — you can run it, but you cannot look inside it.
  • Expression<Func<T,bool>> is data describing code — a tree you can read, inspect and translate into something else, like SQL.
  • That single difference is the whole reason EF Core can turn your C# Where into a SQL WHERE.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Here are two lines that look almost identical:

Func<Order, bool>             a = o => o.Total > 100;
Expression<Func<Order, bool>> b = o => o.Total > 100;

Same lambda on the right. Completely different things on the left.

a is a machine. You can feed an order in and get true or false out. But you cannot ask it "what are you comparing?" or "what number are you checking against?" It is compiled instructions. Opaque.

b is a blueprint of that machine. It is a tree of objects describing the code: "a greater-than comparison, whose left side is the Total property of the parameter, and whose right side is the constant 100." You can walk that tree, read every part, and — crucially — write something else out of it.

Which is exactly what EF Core does. It walks the tree and emits WHERE [Total] > 100.

That is the entire mechanism behind LINQ-to-SQL, and it is why the same Where you write against a List can also run inside your database.

docs.title: What the tree actually looks like
docs.text:
For o => o.Total > 100, the compiler builds this structure:

flowchart TD
    A["LambdaExpression<br/>parameter: o"] --> B["BinaryExpression<br/>NodeType = GreaterThan"]
    B --> C["MemberExpression<br/>property: Total"]
    B --> D["ConstantExpression<br/>value: 100"]
    C --> E["ParameterExpression<br/>name: o, type: Order"]

Every node is a real object you can inspect at runtime:

Expression<Func<Order, bool>> expr = o => o.Total > 100;

var body = (BinaryExpression)expr.Body;

Console.WriteLine(body.NodeType);          // GreaterThan
Console.WriteLine(body.Left);              // o.Total
Console.WriteLine(body.Right);             // 100

var left = (MemberExpression)body.Left;
Console.WriteLine(left.Member.Name);       // "Total"

A database provider does this recursively over the whole tree, mapping each node type to SQL. GreaterThan becomes >, MemberExpression becomes a column name, ConstantExpression becomes a parameter.

docs.title: Why the two overloads exist
docs.text:
Look at the two Where methods:

// LINQ to Objects — works in memory
public static IEnumerable<T> Where<T>(
    this IEnumerable<T> source,
    Func<T, bool> predicate);          // ← compiled code

// LINQ to a query provider — translated
public static IQueryable<T> Where<T>(
    this IQueryable<T> source,
    Expression<Func<T, bool>> predicate);   // ← a tree

The C# compiler picks which one based on the type of the thing you are calling it on. That is why the trap from 2.1 is so easy to fall into:

IQueryable<Order> q = db.Orders;
q.Where(o => o.Total > 100);       // Expression overload → becomes SQL

IEnumerable<Order> e = db.Orders;  // just changing the declared type...
e.Where(o => o.Total > 100);       // ...picks the Func overload → runs in memory

The lambda is identical. The declared type of the variable decided whether your filter ran in the database or after downloading the whole table.

docs.title: You can compile a tree back into code
docs.text:
Expression<Func<Order, bool>> expr = o => o.Total > 100;

Func<Order, bool> compiled = expr.Compile();   // build real executable code
var result = compiled(myOrder);                // now you can run it

Compile() is expensive — it generates IL at runtime. Never call it inside a loop. If you need it repeatedly, compile once and cache the result.

docs.title: Building a tree by hand
docs.text:
You rarely need this, but it is what libraries do when they build queries dynamically:

// Constructing 'o => o.Total > 100' manually
var param    = Expression.Parameter(typeof(Order), "o");
var property = Expression.Property(param, nameof(Order.Total));
var constant = Expression.Constant(100m);
var body     = Expression.GreaterThan(property, constant);

var lambda = Expression.Lambda<Func<Order, bool>>(body, param);

// Usable exactly like a written lambda
var results = db.Orders.Where(lambda).ToList();

This is how dynamic filtering and sorting from user input is implemented — a search screen where the user picks the column and operator.

docs.title: ⚠️ Not everything can be translated
docs.text:
The provider can only translate node types it understands. Your own C# methods are opaque to it:

// This method exists only in .NET. SQL Server has never heard of it.
public static bool IsHighValue(Order o) => o.Total > 1000;

db.Orders.Where(o => IsHighValue(o)).ToList();
// EF Core throws:
//   "The LINQ expression could not be translated"

EF Core sees a MethodCallExpression pointing at your method and has no mapping for it. In older EF versions this would silently fall back to client evaluation — downloading the whole table and filtering in memory. That silent fallback caused so many production disasters that EF Core 3.0 changed it to throw instead. Throwing is the better behaviour: a loud failure at development time beats a quiet one at scale.

Things that typically cannot be translated:

.Where(o => MyHelper(o))                      // your own methods
.Where(o => o.Total.ToString().Length > 3)    // some framework methods
.Where(o => customList.MyExtension(o))        // custom extension methods
.Where(o => o.CreatedAt.ToLocalTime() > x)    // no SQL equivalent

The workaround is to express the logic inline so the provider can see it:

// Instead of a method call, use the expression directly
db.Orders.Where(o => o.Total > 1000);

// Or store the expression so it stays translatable AND reusable
public static Expression<Func<Order, bool>> IsHighValue =>
    o => o.Total > 1000;

db.Orders.Where(IsHighValue);      // works — it is a tree, not compiled code

That last pattern is worth knowing. Storing an Expression<Func<T,bool>> in a static property gives you a named, reusable, still-translatable filter. It is the basis of the Specification pattern — see 22.13.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Dynamic sorting from a user-supplied column name, which is the most common real use:

public static IQueryable<T> OrderByColumn<T>(
    this IQueryable<T> source,
    string columnName,
    bool descending)
{
    // Build:  x => x.<columnName>
    var param    = Expression.Parameter(typeof(T), "x");
    var property = Expression.PropertyOrField(param, columnName);
    var lambda   = Expression.Lambda(property, param);

    // Pick OrderBy or OrderByDescending
    var method = descending ? "OrderByDescending" : "OrderBy";

    // Call it via reflection, because the key type isn't known at compile time
    var call = Expression.Call(
        typeof(Queryable),
        method,
        [typeof(T), property.Type],
        source.Expression,
        Expression.Quote(lambda));

    return source.Provider.CreateQuery<T>(call);
}

Used from a controller:

var page = await _db.Orders
    .Where(o => o.CustomerId == customerId)
    .OrderByColumn(request.SortBy, request.Descending)   // still SQL!
    .Skip(request.Page * 20)
    .Take(20)
    .ToListAsync(ct);

The sort happens in the database, on a column chosen at runtime.

⚠️ PropertyOrField throws if the name does not exist, and the name came from a user. Always validate against an allow-list first — otherwise you have handed users the ability to probe your schema through error messages:

private static readonly HashSet<string> Sortable =
    ["CreatedAt", "Total", "Status"];

if (!Sortable.Contains(request.SortBy))
    throw new ValidationException($"Cannot sort by '{request.SortBy}'");

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between Func<T, bool> and Expression<Func<T, bool>>?

Func<T, bool> is a compiled delegate — you can invoke it, but it is a black box, so nothing can inspect what it does. Expression<Func<T, bool>> is a data structure representing that same lambda as a tree of objects: a comparison node, a property access node, a constant node and so on. Because it is data, a library can walk it and translate it into something else. That is exactly how EF Core turns a C# Where into a SQL WHERE clause. You can turn an expression into a delegate with Compile(), but not the other way round.

Q: How does EF Core turn my LINQ into SQL?

IQueryable<T>'s operators take expression trees rather than delegates, so when you write Where(o => o.Total > 100) the compiler hands EF Core a tree describing that comparison instead of compiled code. Nothing runs at that point — the operators just build up a bigger tree. When you finally enumerate, EF Core's provider walks the tree, maps each node to SQL, and sends one statement to the database. Which overload the compiler chooses depends purely on the static type of the source, which is why declaring something as IEnumerable instead of IQueryable silently moves the work from the database into your process.

Q: Why does EF Core throw "the LINQ expression could not be translated"?

Because the expression tree contains a node the provider cannot map to SQL — most often a call to one of your own methods, which exists only in .NET. Earlier versions of EF Core would silently fall back to fetching everything and filtering in memory, which caused severe performance problems that only appeared at production data volumes. EF Core 3.0 changed this to throw so the problem surfaces during development. The fix is to write the logic inline so the provider can see it, or to store it as an Expression<Func<T,bool>> rather than a normal method, which keeps it translatable and reusable.

Q: When would you build an expression tree by hand?

Mainly for dynamic queries where the shape is not known at compile time — a search or grid screen where the user picks which column to sort or filter by. Building the tree manually lets that sort happen in the database rather than pulling everything back and sorting in memory. It is also how specification-pattern libraries and dynamic filtering libraries work. The important caveat is validation: property names coming from user input must be checked against an allow-list, or you have exposed your schema.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Declaring a variable as IEnumerable instead of IQueryable changes which overload the compiler picks, silently moving work out of the database.
  • Calling your own methods inside a query breaks translation. Express the logic inline or store it as an Expression<Func<T,bool>>.
  • Compile() is expensive — it generates IL at runtime. Never inside a loop.
  • Expression trees can only represent expressions, not statements. No if blocks, no loops, no assignments in a lambda you intend to translate.
  • Building trees from user-supplied names is an injection risk. Validate against an allow-list.
  • Not all providers support the same operators. Something that translates against SQL Server may fail against SQLite or Cosmos.
  • A query that throws "could not be translated" is a good outcome. The alternative — silent client evaluation — is far worse.

docs.title: 2.8 — GroupBy, Join, SelectMany, Aggregate, Zip
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.7 Expression trees · Next: 2.9 First vs Single

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• GroupBy turns a flat list into buckets. Each bucket has a Key and the items in it.
  • Join matches items from two sequences by a shared value — exactly like a SQL inner join.
  • SelectMany flattens. Aggregate folds a sequence into one value. Zip pairs two sequences item by item.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
These five are where LINQ stops being "a nicer foreach" and starts doing things that would take real effort by hand. They also come up in interviews because writing one on a whiteboard shows whether you have used LINQ properly or just Where and Select.

A picture for each:

  • GroupBy — sorting a pile of post into pigeonholes, one per street name.
  • Join — laying two lists side by side and drawing lines between matching IDs.
  • SelectMany — tipping several boxes of items into one big box.
  • Aggregate — a running total, but you decide what "adding" means.
  • Zip — a zip fastener, pairing one tooth from each side.

docs.title: GroupBy — split into buckets
docs.text:
var byCustomer = orders.GroupBy(o => o.CustomerId);

You get back a sequence of groups. Each group is itself a sequence, plus a Key property holding the value you grouped by:

foreach (var group in byCustomer)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Customer {group.Key}:");   // the CustomerId
    foreach (var order in group)                   // the orders for that customer
        Console.WriteLine($"  {order.Id}");
}

That double nature — a group is the items, and has a Key — is the bit people find confusing. In practice you usually project straight into a summary:

var summaries = orders
    .GroupBy(o => o.CustomerId)
    .Select(g => new
    {
        CustomerId = g.Key,               // what you grouped by
        Count      = g.Count(),           // g is the orders in this bucket
        Total      = g.Sum(o => o.Total)
    });

Grouping by more than one value uses an anonymous type or a tuple as the key:

var byMonthAndStatus = orders
    .GroupBy(o => new { o.CreatedAt.Year, o.CreatedAt.Month, o.Status })
    .Select(g => new
    {
        g.Key.Year, g.Key.Month, g.Key.Status,
        Count = g.Count()
    });

That works because anonymous types compare by value (1.22) — two keys with the same contents land in the same bucket.

⚠️ GroupBy reads the entire source before it can produce anything. It cannot know what is in a bucket until it has seen every item. So it is deferred, but not streaming.

docs.title: Join — match two sequences
docs.text:
var result = orders.Join(
    customers,                  // the second sequence
    o => o.CustomerId,          // key from the first
    c => c.Id,                  // key from the second
    (o, c) => new               // what to build from each match
    {
        OrderId  = o.Id,
        Customer = c.Name,
        o.Total
    });

Four arguments, in that order: what to join, key from the left, key from the right, what to produce.

This is an inner join — items with no match on either side are dropped.

Query syntax is genuinely more readable here:

var result = from o in orders
             join c in customers on o.CustomerId equals c.Id
             select new { OrderId = o.Id, Customer = c.Name, o.Total };

For a left join — keep everything from the left even without a match — you use GroupJoin plus SelectMany with DefaultIfEmpty:

var result = from c in customers
             join o in orders on c.Id equals o.CustomerId into customerOrders
             from o in customerOrders.DefaultIfEmpty()      // ← this makes it a LEFT join
             select new
             {
                 Customer = c.Name,
                 OrderId  = o?.Id,          // null when the customer has no orders
                 Total    = o?.Total ?? 0
             };

That DefaultIfEmpty() is the whole trick, and it is worth memorising because "how do you do a left join in LINQ?" is a standard question.

docs.title: SelectMany — flatten
docs.text:
// 3 orders, each with 4 lines

orders.Select(o => o.Lines);        // IEnumerable<List<OrderLine>> — 3 lists
orders.SelectMany(o => o.Lines);    // IEnumerable<OrderLine>       — 12 lines

With the overload that keeps the parent, you can reach both:

var lines = orders.SelectMany(
    o => o.Lines,                          // what to flatten
    (order, line) => new                   // combine parent and child
    {
        order.Id,
        line.Product,
        line.Quantity
    });

docs.title: Aggregate — fold into one value
docs.text:
Sum and Count are specialised aggregations. Aggregate lets you define your own:

// Reimplementing Sum, to show the shape
var total = orders.Aggregate(
    0m,                                // starting value
    (running, order) => running + order.Total);   // how to fold each item in

A more realistic use — building a string:

var names = customers.Aggregate(
    new StringBuilder(),
    (sb, c) => sb.Append(c.Name).Append(", "),
    sb => sb.ToString().TrimEnd(',', ' '));   // optional final transform

⚠️ But do not use Aggregate where a named operator exists. Sum, Max, Count and string.Join are clearer and usually faster. Aggregate is for genuinely custom folds — a running balance with rules, or combining objects in a way no built-in covers.

The empty-sequence trap: the single-argument overload throws on an empty sequence, because it has no starting value to return. Always supply a seed:

new List<int>().Aggregate((a, b) => a + b);   // InvalidOperationException
new List<int>().Aggregate(0, (a, b) => a + b); // 0 — fine

docs.title: Zip — pair two sequences
docs.text:
var names  = new[] { "Ada", "Grace", "Alan" };
var scores = new[] { 90, 95, 88 };

var paired = names.Zip(scores, (n, s) => $"{n}: {s}");
// "Ada: 90", "Grace: 95", "Alan: 88"

// .NET 6+ can produce tuples with no selector
foreach (var (name, score) in names.Zip(scores))
    Console.WriteLine($"{name} scored {score}");

Zip stops at the shorter sequence. Three names and five scores gives three results, silently. If the lengths should match, check first — otherwise you lose data with no error.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic report combining several of these:

public IReadOnlyList<CustomerReport> BuildReport(
    IEnumerable<Order> orders,
    IEnumerable<Customer> customers)
{
    return customers
        // Left join: keep customers even if they have never ordered
        .GroupJoin(
            orders,
            c => c.Id,
            o => o.CustomerId,
            (customer, theirOrders) => new { customer, theirOrders })

        .Select(x => new CustomerReport
        {
            Name       = x.customer.Name,
            OrderCount = x.theirOrders.Count(),

            // Sum over an empty sequence is 0, so no guard needed
            TotalSpent = x.theirOrders.Sum(o => o.Total),

            // Max WOULD throw on empty, so use the null-safe form
            LastOrder  = x.theirOrders.Any()
                            ? x.theirOrders.Max(o => o.CreatedAt)
                            : (DateTime?)null,

            // SelectMany to reach the lines inside the orders
            ItemsBought = x.theirOrders
                           .SelectMany(o => o.Lines)
                           .Sum(l => l.Quantity)
        })
        .OrderByDescending(r => r.TotalSpent)
        .ToList();
}

Note the asymmetry called out in the comments: Sum on an empty sequence returns zero, but Max and Min and Average throw. That inconsistency catches people constantly, and it is exactly the kind of detail an interviewer probes.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does GroupBy return?

A sequence of groups, where each group implements IGrouping<TKey, TElement>. That interface is itself an IEnumerable of the items in the group, plus a Key property holding the value you grouped by. So a group both is the items and has the key. In practice you almost always follow it with a Select that projects the key and some aggregate over the group into a summary object. Worth knowing that GroupBy has to read the whole source before it can emit anything, since it cannot know what belongs in a bucket otherwise.

Q: How do you do a left join in LINQ?

Join is always an inner join, so unmatched items on either side disappear. For a left join you use GroupJoin, which gives you each left item together with a collection of its matches — possibly empty — and then SelectMany with DefaultIfEmpty(), which yields a null for groups that had no match. In query syntax that is join ... into g followed by from x in g.DefaultIfEmpty(). The DefaultIfEmpty is the part that actually makes it a left join.

Q: What is the difference between Select and SelectMany?

Select produces exactly one output per input, so if the thing you project is a collection you end up with a sequence of collections. SelectMany does the same projection but flattens the results into a single sequence. With three orders of four lines each, Select gives you three lists and SelectMany gives you twelve lines. There is also an overload that passes both the parent and the child to your projection, which is how you keep the order ID alongside each line.

Q: When would you use Aggregate?

Only when there is no named operator for what you need. Sum, Count, Max and string.Join are all specialised aggregations and they are clearer and usually faster, so reaching for Aggregate to reimplement them is a readability regression. It earns its place for genuinely custom folds — computing a running balance with business rules, or combining objects in a way nothing built-in covers. The trap is that the overload without a seed throws on an empty sequence, so I always supply an explicit starting value.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Sum returns 0 on an empty sequence, but Max, Min and Average throw. Guard with Any() or use the nullable overloads.
  • Aggregate without a seed throws on an empty sequence. Always pass a starting value.
  • Zip silently stops at the shorter sequence. No error, just missing data.
  • Join is an inner join. Unmatched items on both sides vanish, which can look like data loss.
  • GroupBy buffers the entire source. It is deferred, but it cannot stream.
  • GroupBy in EF Core does not always translate. Complex groupings can fall back or throw; check the generated SQL. See 13.15.
  • Grouping by a class without value equality puts every item in its own bucket. Use an anonymous type, a tuple, or a record as the key.
  • Reusing Aggregate where Sum exists is slower and harder to read.

docs.title: 2.9 — First vs FirstOrDefault vs Single vs SingleOrDefault
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.8 Advanced LINQ operators · Next: 2.10 Threads vs Tasks

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• First = "give me the first match, and there had better be one."
  • Single = "there must be exactly one match — throw if there are none or more than one."
  • ...OrDefault = "return null instead of throwing when there is nothing."
  • Single is slower, because to prove there is only one it must keep looking after it finds one.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
All four answer "get me one item from this sequence". They differ in what counts as wrong.

Think of it as asking a room full of people a question:

  • First — "someone put your hand up." You take the first hand you see and stop looking. If nobody responds, that is an error.
  • FirstOrDefault — same, but if nobody responds you shrug and carry on with nothing.
  • Single — "exactly one of you should have your hand up." You must scan the whole room to be sure nobody else did. Two hands is an error. Zero hands is an error.
  • SingleOrDefault — same scan, but zero hands is acceptable. Two is still an error.

That "scan the whole room" difference is the performance point, and it is the half of the answer most candidates miss.

docs.title: The four in a table
docs.text:
Method 0 matches 1 match 2+ matches Stops early? First() throws returns it returns the first ✅ FirstOrDefault() null / default returns it returns the first ✅ Single() throws returns it throws ❌ SingleOrDefault() null / default returns it throws ❌

Both First variants stop the moment they find a match. Both Single variants keep going, because finding a second match is the only way to know it should throw.

var orders = new List<Order> { a, b, c };

orders.First();                          // a
orders.First(o => o.Total > 1_000_000);  // InvalidOperationException:
                                         //   "Sequence contains no matching element"

orders.FirstOrDefault(o => o.Total > 1_000_000);   // null

orders.Single();                         // InvalidOperationException:
                                         //   "Sequence contains more than one element"
orders.Single(o => o.Id == a.Id);        // a — exactly one match, fine

docs.title: The performance difference, concretely
docs.text:
// A table with 1,000,000 orders, one matching row

db.Orders.First(o => o.Id == id);
// SQL: SELECT TOP 1 * FROM Orders WHERE Id = @id
// Stops at the first row found.

db.Orders.Single(o => o.Id == id);
// SQL: SELECT TOP 2 * FROM Orders WHERE Id = @id
// Fetches TWO rows so it can tell whether a second one exists.

TOP 2 rather than TOP 1. On an indexed primary key the difference is trivial. On an unindexed column where the match is rare, Single may scan a great deal more.

docs.title: default is not always null
docs.text:
...OrDefault returns default(T), which depends on the type (1.1):

List<Order> empty = [];
empty.FirstOrDefault();          // null — Order is a class

List<int> emptyInts = [];
emptyInts.FirstOrDefault();      // 0 — NOT null! int is a value type

That second case is a genuine bug source:

var total = amounts.FirstOrDefault();
if (total == 0)
{
    // Is this "nothing found" or "found a zero"?
    // You cannot tell. They are indistinguishable.
}

Fixes:

// .NET 6+ — supply your own fallback
var total = amounts.FirstOrDefault(-1);

// Or make the sequence nullable so null means "missing"
int? total = amounts.Cast<int?>().FirstOrDefault();

// Or check separately
if (amounts.Any())
    var total = amounts.First();

docs.title: The related pair: Last and ElementAt
docs.text:
orders.Last();                   // throws if empty
orders.LastOrDefault();          // null if empty
orders.ElementAt(3);             // throws if out of range
orders.ElementAtOrDefault(3);    // null if out of range

⚠️ Last() on an IEnumerable walks the entire sequence to reach the end. Against a database, prefer OrderByDescending(...).First() — that becomes ORDER BY ... DESC TOP 1, which the database can satisfy from an index.

docs.title: Which to use
docs.text:
The choice should describe what you believe about your data, and that is the answer an interviewer is listening for.

// Looking up by primary key — exactly one row must exist, or the data is corrupt.
// Single documents that expectation and will tell you loudly if it breaks.
var order = await db.Orders.SingleAsync(o => o.Id == id, ct);

// Looking up by a unique-ish key that may legitimately be missing
var user = await db.Users.SingleOrDefaultAsync(u => u.Email == email, ct);
if (user is null) return NotFound();

// Getting the newest of many — several exist, you want one
var latest = await db.Orders
    .Where(o => o.CustomerId == id)
    .OrderByDescending(o => o.CreatedAt)
    .FirstAsync(ct);

// Optional lookup where absence is normal
var discount = discounts.FirstOrDefault(d => d.Code == code);
var amount   = discount?.Amount ?? 0;

The rule: use Single when more than one would mean a bug. It is a runtime assertion of a data invariant. Using First there would silently pick one and hide the duplicate, possibly for years.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The pattern that shows up constantly in ASP.NET Core controllers:

[HttpGet("{id:guid}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Get(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // SingleOrDefault: the ID is a primary key so at most one row can match,
    // but the client may well ask for one that does not exist.
    var order = await _db.Orders
        .AsNoTracking()
        .SingleOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id, ct);

    if (order is null)
        return NotFound();          // a normal outcome, not an exception

    return Ok(_mapper.ToDto(order));
}

Why not First here? Because if a duplicate ID ever appeared, First would quietly return one of them and you would never find out. Single turns that into a loud failure.

Why not Single (without OrDefault)? Because "the client asked for an ID that does not exist" is normal traffic, not an error. Throwing an exception for it would be using exceptions for control flow, which is slow and noisy in your logs (1.20).

The general shape: SingleOrDefault plus an explicit null check plus a 404.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between First and Single?

First returns the first matching item and stops looking, throwing only if there are no matches at all. Single insists there is exactly one match — it throws if there are none and also if there is more than one. Because it has to prove uniqueness, it cannot stop at the first match; it keeps reading to check nothing else qualifies. Against a database that shows up as TOP 2 instead of TOP 1. So they differ both in meaning and in cost.

Q: When would you choose Single over First?

When more than one match would mean the data is wrong. Looking a row up by its primary key is the clearest case — two rows with the same key means something is broken, and I want to know rather than silently work with an arbitrary one of them. Single acts as a runtime assertion of that invariant. If several matches are legitimate and I just want one of them — the most recent order, say — then First after an OrderBy is correct and cheaper.

Q: What does FirstOrDefault return for a list of int?

Zero, not null, because default(int) is zero. That is a real trap, because you then cannot distinguish "nothing matched" from "matched a value that happens to be zero". The fixes are to pass an explicit fallback using the .NET 6 overload, to project to a nullable type so null genuinely means missing, or to check Any() separately before calling First.

Q: Which would you use in a controller looking up by ID, and why?

SingleOrDefault, followed by an explicit null check returning 404. Single documents that the ID is unique, so a duplicate would throw rather than silently return one row. The OrDefault part matters because a client requesting a non-existent ID is completely normal traffic — turning that into an exception would be using exceptions for control flow, which is expensive and fills your logs with errors that are not errors.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• First() on an empty sequence throws, it does not return null. The exception message — "Sequence contains no elements" — tells you nothing about which query failed.
  • FirstOrDefault() on a value type returns 0 or false, not null. You cannot tell "missing" from "legitimately zero".
  • Single costs more than First. It must keep reading to prove uniqueness.
  • Using First where Single belongs hides duplicate data, potentially for years.
  • Last() on an IEnumerable walks the whole sequence. Use OrderByDescending(...).First() against a database.
  • The exception messages are unhelpfully generic. In a method with several queries you cannot tell which one threw. Prefer SingleOrDefault plus your own descriptive exception.
  • Use the Async versions with EF Core — SingleOrDefaultAsync, FirstOrDefaultAsync. The synchronous ones block a thread. See 2.13.

docs.title: 2.10 — Threads, ThreadPool, Task vs Thread
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.9 First vs Single · Next: 2.11 async/await internals

Markers: 🔥 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A thread is an actual worker provided by the operating system. Creating one is expensive — about 1 MB of memory each.
  • The thread pool is a reusable set of threads .NET keeps around, so you do not pay that cost every time.
  • A Task is not a thread. It is a promise of a future result. Some tasks use a thread; many use none at all.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
These three words get used interchangeably and they are not the same thing at all.

A thread is a worker. The operating system gives your process workers, and each one can execute code. Hiring one is slow and each costs roughly a megabyte of memory for its stack.

The thread pool is an agency. Rather than hiring and firing workers constantly, .NET keeps a pool of them. You hand it work, an idle worker picks it up, and when they finish they go back to the pool instead of being dismissed.

A Task is a job ticket. It represents work that will eventually produce a result. It says nothing about who does the work. Some tickets are handed to a pool worker. Others are given to a device — a disk or a network card — which does the work with no worker involved at all.

That last point is the one interviews are really testing, and it is the difference between understanding async and just using it.

docs.title: Creating a raw thread — rarely correct now
docs.text:
var thread = new Thread(() =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("running on my own thread");
});
thread.Start();
thread.Join();      // wait for it to finish

Costs: about 1 MB of stack memory, plus roughly a millisecond to create and destroy. Spawn a thousand and you have used a gigabyte of memory doing nothing useful.

You would only create a raw Thread deliberately when you need something the pool cannot give you — a dedicated long-running loop, a specific priority, a foreground thread that keeps the process alive, or a specific apartment state for COM interop.

docs.title: The thread pool
docs.text:
ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(_ => Console.WriteLine("running on a pool thread"));

// Task.Run is the modern way to do the same thing
Task.Run(() => Console.WriteLine("running on a pool thread"));

The pool reuses threads, grows when work queues up, and shrinks when it goes quiet. Because threads are recycled, you must never leave one in a broken state — do not change its culture or priority and forget to restore it.

docs.title: The crucial part: a Task is not a thread
docs.text:
Two tasks. One uses a thread; the other does not.

// CPU-bound: there IS real computing to do,
// so a pool thread runs it.
var sum = await Task.Run(() =>
{
    var total = 0;
    for (var i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) total += i;
    return total;
});

// I/O-bound: NO thread is used while waiting.
var response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://example.com");

For the second one, here is what actually happens:

  1. Your code calls GetAsync.
  2. The request is handed to the operating system's network stack.
  3. Your thread returns to the pool and serves other work.
  4. Time passes — maybe 200 milliseconds. Zero threads are involved. The network card is doing the work.
  5. The response arrives. The OS signals completion.
  6. A thread is taken from the pool to continue your method after the await.

There is no thread sitting and waiting. This is the single most important idea in async programming, and the reason it scales.

flowchart TD
    A["Request arrives"] --> B["Pool thread picks it up"]
    B --> C["await httpClient.GetAsync"]
    C --> D["Thread RETURNS TO POOL<br/>and serves other requests"]
    D -.->|"200ms passes<br/>NO thread used"| E["Network card signals<br/>response arrived"]
    E --> F["A pool thread resumes<br/>the method"]
    F --> G["Response sent"]

docs.title: Why this matters for a web server
docs.text:
Imagine 1,000 concurrent requests, each waiting 200 ms on a database.

Blocking (synchronous): each request holds a thread for the whole 200 ms. You need 1,000 threads. At ~1 MB each that is a gigabyte of stack memory, plus the CPU cost of the OS switching between them constantly. The default pool will not grow that fast, so requests queue and latency collapses.

Async: each request releases its thread while waiting. A handful of threads serve all 1,000 requests, because at any instant almost none of them need a worker — they are all just waiting on the database.

That is the entire reason ASP.NET Core is async throughout. Not to make one request faster — an async request is very slightly slower — but to serve far more requests with the same hardware.

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text: Situation Use Waiting for I/O — network, disk, database await the async method directly Real CPU work you want off the current thread Task.Run(...) A long-running dedicated loop Thread with IsBackground = true, or a BackgroundService Background work in ASP.NET Core BackgroundService (21.1)

docs.title: ⚠️ Do not wrap I/O in Task.Run
docs.text:
// WRONG — pointless and harmful
var data = await Task.Run(() => httpClient.GetAsync(url).Result);

This takes a pool thread, blocks it on .Result for the whole network call, and gains nothing. You have converted efficient thread-free waiting back into thread-blocking waiting, and added an extra thread hop.

// RIGHT
var data = await httpClient.GetAsync(url);

The rule: Task.Run is for CPU work. For I/O, await the async method directly.

And in ASP.NET Core specifically, Task.Run is usually wrong even for CPU work — the request is already on a pool thread, so moving the work to another pool thread just adds overhead without freeing anything. It helps in desktop apps, where it gets work off the single UI thread.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
public class ReportService(HttpClient http, AppDbContext db)
{
    public async Task<Report> BuildAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // I/O — awaited directly. No thread held while these wait.
        // WhenAll runs them concurrently, so total time is the SLOWEST,
        // not the sum. See 2.12.
        var ordersTask = db.Orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == id).ToListAsync(ct);
        var ratesTask  = http.GetFromJsonAsync<Rates>("/rates", ct);

        await Task.WhenAll(ordersTask, ratesTask);

        var orders = await ordersTask;
        var rates  = await ratesTask;

        // Genuinely CPU-heavy work over a large result set.
        // Task.Run is defensible here IF this takes long enough to matter.
        var stats = await Task.Run(() => ComputeStatistics(orders, rates), ct);

        return new Report(orders.Count, stats);
    }

    private static Statistics ComputeStatistics(List<Order> orders, Rates rates)
    {
        // ... heavy number crunching over hundreds of thousands of rows ...
    }
}

Note the honesty in that comment. If ComputeStatistics takes 2 milliseconds, Task.Run is pure overhead — just call it directly. It only earns its place when the work is long enough that occupying a request thread genuinely hurts throughput.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between a Thread and a Task?

A Thread is an actual operating system worker with its own stack, costing about a megabyte of memory and a millisecond or so to create. A Task is a much higher-level thing — it represents an operation that will complete in the future and produce a result. Crucially, a task does not imply a thread. Task.Run does hand work to a thread-pool thread, but an async I/O operation like an HTTP call uses no thread at all while it waits — the work is done by the network hardware and the operating system, and a thread is only needed again once the result arrives.

Q: If await doesn't use a thread while waiting, what is actually happening?

The operation is handed down to the operating system, which registers a completion callback with the device driver. Your thread is then free and goes back to the pool to serve other work. When the data arrives, the OS signals completion and the runtime schedules the rest of your method onto an available pool thread. So during the wait there genuinely is no thread associated with the operation — that is why a server with a handful of threads can handle thousands of concurrent requests that are all waiting on a database.

Q: Why is ASP.NET Core async all the way through?

Throughput, not speed. An individual async request is marginally slower than a synchronous one because of the state machine overhead. But because threads are released during I/O waits, a small pool can serve a very large number of concurrent requests. Synchronously, each in-flight request pins a thread for its entire duration, so a thousand concurrent requests need a thousand threads — around a gigabyte of stack plus heavy context switching. Async turns that into a handful of threads.

Q: When should you use Task.Run?

For genuinely CPU-bound work that you want off the current thread, and mainly in desktop applications where it keeps the UI thread responsive. In ASP.NET Core it is usually the wrong answer, because the request is already running on a pool thread — moving work to another pool thread adds a hop without freeing any capacity. And you should never wrap an I/O call in it, because that blocks a pool thread on something that was designed not to need one.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "A Task runs on a separate thread." Not necessarily, and usually not for I/O. This is the most common misconception in the whole topic.
  • Wrapping I/O in Task.Run converts thread-free waiting back into thread-blocking waiting.
  • Task.Run in ASP.NET Core rarely helps. You are already on a pool thread.
  • Creating raw threads for short work is very wasteful. ~1 MB and ~1 ms each.
  • Pool threads are recycled. Changing culture, priority or thread-local state without restoring it leaks that change into unrelated later work.
  • Thread.Sleep blocks a thread; Task.Delay does not. Never use Thread.Sleep in async code.
  • Blocking pool threads causes thread-pool starvation — the pool only adds new threads slowly, so latency spikes badly under load. See 19.12.
