docs.title: 2.11 — async / await: The State Machine Underneath
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.10 Threads vs Tasks · Next: 2.12 Task vs ValueTask

Markers: 🔥 🎯 🧠 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• async/await is compiler magic, not runtime magic. The compiler chops your method into pieces and rebuilds it as a state machine class.
  • await means "if this isn't finished, return to my caller now, and resume here later."
  • The method returns at the first incomplete await. Everything after that runs as a callback.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
await looks like it pauses your method. It does not — pausing would mean a thread sitting idle, which is exactly what async exists to avoid.

What actually happens is closer to leaving a bookmark and walking away.

Imagine reading a long book, and partway through you have to wait for a delivery. Instead of standing at the door doing nothing, you put a bookmark in, close the book, and go do something else. When the delivery arrives, someone — not necessarily you — picks the book up at the bookmark and carries on.

That is await. The bookmark is a state number. Closing the book is returning to your caller. Picking it up again is a callback when the operation completes.

The compiler builds all of this for you. Understanding that it is compile-time rewriting, not some runtime trick, is what makes the rest of async make sense.

docs.title: What you write
docs.text:
public async Task<int> GetTotalAsync(Guid id)
{
    var orders = await _db.GetOrdersAsync(id);      // pause point 1
    var rates  = await _http.GetRatesAsync();       // pause point 2
    return orders.Sum(o => o.Total * rates.Usd);
}

docs.title: What the compiler produces
docs.text:
Roughly this — a class with a MoveNext method and a state number:

// Compiler-generated, simplified heavily
class GetTotalAsyncStateMachine : IAsyncStateMachine
{
    public int _state = -1;
    public AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<int> _builder;
    public Guid id;                                 // parameters become FIELDS

    private List<Order> _orders;                    // locals become FIELDS too
    private Rates _rates;
    private TaskAwaiter<List<Order>> _awaiter1;
    private TaskAwaiter<Rates> _awaiter2;

    public void MoveNext()
    {
        switch (_state)
        {
            case -1:                                // first entry
                _awaiter1 = _db.GetOrdersAsync(id).GetAwaiter();
                if (!_awaiter1.IsCompleted)
                {
                    _state = 0;
                    _awaiter1.OnCompleted(MoveNext); // "call me back, then RETURN"
                    return;                          // ← the method exits HERE
                }
                goto case 0;

            case 0:                                 // resumed after await 1
                _orders = _awaiter1.GetResult();
                _awaiter2 = _http.GetRatesAsync().GetAwaiter();
                if (!_awaiter2.IsCompleted)
                {
                    _state = 1;
                    _awaiter2.OnCompleted(MoveNext);
                    return;
                }
                goto case 1;

            case 1:                                 // resumed after await 2
                _rates = _awaiter2.GetResult();
                _builder.SetResult(_orders.Sum(o => o.Total * _rates.Usd));
                return;
        }
    }
}

Three things worth pulling out of that:

  1. Your locals became fields. They have to survive between calls to MoveNext, so they move onto the heap. That is why a value type held across an await lives on the heap — see 1.1.
  2. return happens at the first incomplete await. The method genuinely exits and control goes back to the caller. Nothing is blocked.
  3. OnCompleted(MoveNext) is a callback registration. "When you finish, call me again, and I will pick up at the state I saved."

docs.title: The fast path
docs.text:
Notice if (!_awaiter1.IsCompleted). If the operation already finished — a cache hit, a buffered stream read — there is no state saved, no callback, no return. Execution falls straight through synchronously.

This is a deliberate optimisation and it matters: it is why an async method that usually completes immediately is cheap, and it is the reason ValueTask exists (2.12).

docs.title: async on the signature does nothing by itself
docs.text:
public async Task<int> Foo()      // 'async' is NOT part of the public contract

async is an instruction to the compiler, not information for callers. It says "rewrite this method into a state machine and let me use await inside it". Callers only see Task<int>.

That is why you can override a non-async method with an async one, and why removing async while returning the task directly is a valid optimisation:

// With async: builds a state machine to await and re-wrap
public async Task<Order> GetAsync(Guid id)
    => await _repo.GetAsync(id);

// Without: just passes the task straight through. No state machine at all.
public Task<Order> GetAsync(Guid id)
    => _repo.GetAsync(id);

The second is slightly faster. But be careful — without async, exceptions thrown before the task is returned propagate synchronously rather than being captured in the task, and using blocks dispose immediately rather than after the operation completes. Only elide async when the method body is a single pass-through return.

docs.title: The three return types
docs.text: Return type Use for Task An async method that returns nothing Task<T> An async method that returns a value void Only event handlers. See 2.15 — it is otherwise a bug

docs.title: The full picture 🎯
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant M as Your async method
    participant OS as OS / device

    C->>M: GetTotalAsync(id)
    M->>OS: start the database read
    Note over M: awaiter not complete<br/>save state = 0<br/>register callback
    M-->>C: returns an incomplete Task
    Note over C: caller carries on<br/>THREAD IS FREE
    Note over OS: 50 ms passes<br/>no thread involved
    OS-->>M: data ready → MoveNext()
    Note over M: resume at state 0<br/>run to completion
    M-->>C: Task transitions to completed

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The cost of the state machine is real but small, and worth knowing when it matters:

// Allocates: a state machine box + a Task object, every call
public async Task<int> GetCountAsync(Guid id)
{
    var cached = _cache.Get(id);
    if (cached is not null) return cached.Value;    // usually hits here!

    return await _db.CountAsync(id);
}

If that cache hits 99% of the time, you are allocating a Task<int> on nearly every call for a value you already had. ValueTask avoids it:

public ValueTask<int> GetCountAsync(Guid id)
{
    var cached = _cache.Get(id);
    if (cached is not null)
        return new ValueTask<int>(cached.Value);    // no allocation

    return new ValueTask<int>(_db.CountAsync(id));  // falls back to a real Task
}

Only do this after measuring. For a method called a few hundred times per second, the allocation is irrelevant and Task is clearer. See 2.12.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What does the compiler do with an async method?

It rewrites it into a state machine. The method body is split at each await into segments, and those become cases in a switch inside a generated MoveNext method. Your local variables and parameters become fields on that generated class so they survive across the pause points. At each await, the compiler checks whether the operation has already completed — if so it falls straight through, and if not it saves the current state number, registers MoveNext as a completion callback, and returns to the caller. So the method genuinely exits at the first incomplete await and the rest runs later as a callback.

Q: What actually happens when you hit an await?

The awaited operation is started, and the awaiter is asked whether it is already complete. If it is, execution continues synchronously with no overhead at all. If not, the state machine records where it got to, hooks MoveNext up as a callback on the operation, and returns an incomplete Task to the caller — which frees the thread to do other work. When the operation finishes, the callback fires, MoveNext runs again, and it resumes at the saved state.

Q: Where do local variables live in an async method?

On the heap, inside the generated state machine object — at least any that are used after an await. They cannot stay on the stack, because the stack frame disappears when the method returns at the pause point. This is why you cannot use a Span<T> across an await: spans are stack-only by design and cannot be stored in a heap object. It is also why capturing large objects in an async method keeps them alive for the whole operation.

Q: Does async change the method's signature?

No. async is a compiler directive, not part of the contract. It tells the compiler to build a state machine and permits await inside the body, but callers only ever see the return type. That is why you can implement a non-async interface method with an async one, and why you can sometimes remove async and return the task directly as a small optimisation — though only for a straight pass-through, because dropping async changes how exceptions and using blocks behave.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "await pauses the thread." It does the opposite — it releases the thread and returns to the caller.
  • Locals move to the heap. So a Span<T> cannot cross an await, and captured objects stay alive for the whole operation.
  • The state machine allocates. Usually irrelevant, but measurable in very hot paths — that is what ValueTask addresses.
  • Removing async for a pass-through changes exception timing. Without async, an exception thrown before the task is returned propagates synchronously instead of being captured in the task.
  • Never elide async around a using. Without async the dispose runs before the operation completes, closing the resource too early.
  • async void cannot be awaited and its exceptions crash the process. See 2.15.
  • An async method that never awaits runs entirely synchronously and the compiler warns you — the state machine overhead is paid for nothing.

docs.title: 2.12 — Task vs ValueTask, WhenAll, WhenAny, Task.Run
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.11 async/await internals · Next: 2.13 Async deadlocks

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Task.WhenAll runs several operations at once and waits for all. It is the single biggest easy performance win in async code.
  • Task.WhenAny returns as soon as the first one finishes — use it for timeouts and racing.
  • ValueTask avoids an allocation when a method usually completes immediately. Only reach for it after measuring, and never await it twice.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
An await on its own is sequential. Three awaits in a row means waiting three times, one after another:

var a = await GetAAsync();     // 200 ms
var b = await GetBAsync();     // 200 ms
var c = await GetCAsync();     // 200 ms
// Total: 600 ms

Each one starts only after the previous finished. But if they do not depend on each other, that is wasted time — you could have had all three in flight at once.

A picture: putting a kettle on, then toast in the toaster, then eggs on the hob. You do not stand and watch the kettle boil before touching the toaster. You start all three and then collect them as they finish. Task.WhenAll is exactly that.

var taskA = GetAAsync();       // started
var taskB = GetBAsync();       // started
var taskC = GetCAsync();       // started — all three running now

await Task.WhenAll(taskA, taskB, taskC);
// Total: 200 ms — the slowest one, not the sum

Three times faster for a two-line change. This comes up in interviews constantly because it is such a common missed optimisation in real code.

docs.title: Task.WhenAll
docs.text:
public async Task<Dashboard> LoadAsync(Guid userId, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // Start them all. Note: NO await on these lines — that is the point.
    var ordersTask   = _orders.GetForUserAsync(userId, ct);
    var profileTask  = _users.GetProfileAsync(userId, ct);
    var messagesTask = _messages.GetUnreadAsync(userId, ct);

    await Task.WhenAll(ordersTask, profileTask, messagesTask);

    // Now retrieve the results — these are already complete, so no waiting
    return new Dashboard(
        await ordersTask,
        await profileTask,
        await messagesTask);
}

The critical detail: do not await on the lines that start the tasks. Writing var orders = await _orders.GetForUserAsync(...) makes it sequential again. The tasks must be started first and awaited afterwards.

There is a typed version that returns an array of results:

var results = await Task.WhenAll(ids.Select(id => FetchAsync(id, ct)));
// results is T[] in the same order as the input

⚠️ Do not fire off unbounded WhenAll over a large collection. A thousand simultaneous HTTP calls will exhaust connections and probably get you rate-limited. Batch it:

// Limit to 10 at a time
var throttle = new SemaphoreSlim(10);

var tasks = ids.Select(async id =>
{
    await throttle.WaitAsync(ct);
    try   { return await FetchAsync(id, ct); }
    finally { throttle.Release(); }
});

var results = await Task.WhenAll(tasks);

Or in .NET 6+, Parallel.ForEachAsync does this for you — see 2.19.

docs.title: Task.WhenAll and exceptions
docs.text:
If several tasks fail, WhenAll throws only the first exception when you await it. The rest are still there, on the returned task:

var all = Task.WhenAll(t1, t2, t3);
try
{
    await all;                     // throws only the FIRST exception
}
catch (Exception)
{
    // Get them ALL from the task itself
    foreach (var ex in all.Exception!.InnerExceptions)
        _logger.LogError(ex, "Task failed");
}

Also worth knowing: WhenAll waits for every task even if one fails early. It does not cancel the others. If you want that, pass a linked CancellationTokenSource.

docs.title: Task.WhenAny — first one wins
docs.text:
var work    = DoWorkAsync(ct);
var timeout = Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5), ct);

var finished = await Task.WhenAny(work, timeout);

if (finished == timeout)
    throw new TimeoutException("Took longer than 5 seconds");

var result = await work;      // await again to get the value or rethrow

⚠️ WhenAny does not cancel the losers. In the example above, DoWorkAsync keeps running after the timeout — it just goes unobserved. Always pass a CancellationToken so you can actually stop it.

Note that .NET 6 added a much simpler way to do exactly this timeout:

await work.WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5), ct);   // throws TimeoutException

Prefer that. WhenAny is for genuine racing — querying three mirrors and taking whichever answers first.

docs.title: Task vs ValueTask
docs.text:
Task is a class, so returning one allocates an object on the heap. For a method called millions of times that usually completes immediately, those allocations add up.

ValueTask is a struct. When the result is already available, no allocation happens at all.

public ValueTask<User> GetUserAsync(Guid id)
{
    if (_cache.TryGetValue(id, out var cached))
        return new ValueTask<User>(cached);      // NO allocation — the common path

    return new ValueTask<User>(LoadFromDbAsync(id));   // wraps a real Task
}

The rules for ValueTask, and these are strict:

Rule Why Await it only once The underlying object may be recycled after the first await Do not use .Result or .Wait() Undefined behaviour on an incomplete ValueTask Do not pass it to WhenAll/WhenAny Call .AsTask() first Do not store it in a field Same recycling problem 
var vt = GetUserAsync(id);
var a = await vt;
var b = await vt;      // UNDEFINED BEHAVIOUR — may throw or return garbage

If you need any of the forbidden things, call .AsTask() once and use that.

When to use each:

  • Task — the default. Always correct, easy to reason about.
  • ValueTask — only when a method is very hot and usually completes synchronously, and you have measured a real benefit. It is a library-author optimisation, not something to sprinkle through application code.

docs.title: Task.Run
docs.text:
Covered in 2.10, but the summary:

await Task.Run(() => HeavyComputation());   // CPU-bound: reasonable
await Task.Run(() => http.GetAsync(url));   // I/O: WRONG — just await it directly

docs.title: Task.FromResult and friends
docs.text:
For returning an already-known value from a method with an async signature:

public Task<int> GetAsync() => Task.FromResult(42);
public Task DoNothingAsync() => Task.CompletedTask;      // no allocation, cached
public Task<int> FailAsync() => Task.FromException<int>(new InvalidOperationException());

Task.CompletedTask is a cached singleton — always use it rather than Task.FromResult<object>(null).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The realistic before-and-after, and the shape to recognise in a code review:

// BEFORE — 3 sequential round trips. ~600 ms.
public async Task<OrderPageModel> GetPageAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var order    = await _orders.GetAsync(id, ct);           // 200 ms
    var customer = await _customers.GetAsync(order.CustomerId, ct);  // 200 ms
    var related  = await _orders.GetRelatedAsync(id, ct);    // 200 ms

    return new OrderPageModel(order, customer, related);
}

Look at the dependency: customer needs order.CustomerId, so those two genuinely must be sequential. But related only needs id, which we had from the start.

// AFTER — ~400 ms. The independent call runs alongside the chain.
public async Task<OrderPageModel> GetPageAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var relatedTask = _orders.GetRelatedAsync(id, ct);       // start it NOW

    var order    = await _orders.GetAsync(id, ct);           // 200 ms
    var customer = await _customers.GetAsync(order.CustomerId, ct);  // 200 ms

    return new OrderPageModel(order, customer, await relatedTask);   // already done
}

The technique: look at each await and ask "does this actually need the previous result?" Anything that does not can be started earlier.

⚠️ One caveat specific to EF Core: a single DbContext cannot run two queries at the same time. Doing so throws "A second operation was started on this context instance". If the parallel calls share a context, you need separate contexts via IDbContextFactory. See 13.2.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How do you run several async operations concurrently?

Start them without awaiting, then await them together with Task.WhenAll. The mistake is writing var a = await FooAsync() on each line, which makes them sequential — each one only starts after the previous finished. If you capture the tasks first and await afterwards, they all run at once and the total time is the slowest one rather than the sum. For three 200-millisecond calls that turns 600 milliseconds into 200.

Q: What happens to exceptions with Task.WhenAll?

Awaiting the combined task rethrows only the first exception, which is easy to miss if several tasks failed. The others are still available through the Exception property on the task itself, which is an AggregateException holding all of them. So if I need to log everything, I keep a reference to the combined task and inspect InnerExceptions in the catch block. Worth adding that WhenAll waits for every task even after one fails — it does not cancel the rest.

Q: What is ValueTask and when would you use it?

Task is a class, so returning one allocates. ValueTask is a struct, so a method that usually has its result already — a cache hit, a buffered read — can return without allocating. The trade-off is a set of strict rules: you may only await it once, you must not block on it, and you cannot pass it to WhenAll without calling AsTask first, because the underlying object may be pooled and reused after the first await. It is a library-level optimisation for genuinely hot paths, and I would only introduce it after profiling showed the allocations mattered.

Q: How do you put a timeout on an async operation?

In .NET 6 and later, task.WaitAsync(timespan), which throws a TimeoutException if it takes too long. Before that, the pattern was Task.WhenAny with a Task.Delay and then checking which one won. The important caveat with either approach is that timing out does not stop the underlying work — it carries on running unobserved. So you also want to pass a CancellationToken that you cancel, otherwise you have a timeout that frees the caller but leaks the operation.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• await on the line that starts each task makes them sequential. Capture the tasks first, await afterwards.
  • WhenAll rethrows only the first exception. Inspect task.Exception.InnerExceptions for the rest.
  • WhenAll does not cancel remaining tasks when one fails. They all run to completion.
  • WhenAny does not cancel the losers. Pass a CancellationToken or they leak.
  • Awaiting a ValueTask twice is undefined behaviour. So is blocking on one.
  • Unbounded WhenAll over a large collection exhausts connections. Throttle with SemaphoreSlim or use Parallel.ForEachAsync.
  • Two concurrent queries on one DbContext throw. Use IDbContextFactory for parallel database work.
  • An unobserved failed task used to crash the process. It no longer does by default, but the exception is silently swallowed — which is arguably worse.

docs.title: 2.13 — Deadlocks: .Result, .Wait() and ConfigureAwait(false)
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.12 Task vs ValueTask · Next: 2.14 CancellationToken

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Never call .Result or .Wait() on a task. In some apps it deadlocks permanently; in ASP.NET Core it wastes a thread and can bring the server down under load.
  • The classic deadlock happens when a thread blocks waiting for work that needs that same thread to finish.
  • ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so it cannot deadlock this way — but blocking is still harmful, and ConfigureAwait(false) still matters in libraries.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
A deadlock is two things each waiting for the other, so neither can ever proceed.

The async version is subtler and more absurd: one thread waiting for itself.

A picture: you are the only person working in a shop. A customer asks you to fetch something from the stockroom. You say "I'll wait right here at the till until someone brings it out" — but you are the only one who can go and get it. You will stand there forever.

That is exactly what .Result does in an app with a synchronization context. The thread blocks waiting for the async work to complete, but the async work's continuation is queued to run on that very thread, which is busy blocking. Nothing can ever move.

docs.title: What a synchronization context is
docs.text:
Some frameworks require certain code to run on a specific thread. A desktop UI is the classic example — only the UI thread may touch controls, or the framework throws.

The synchronization context is the mechanism that enforces this. When you await in such an app, the continuation is not run on just any thread; it is posted back to the context so it resumes on the original thread.

Framework Has a synchronization context? WinForms / WPF ✅ Yes — the UI thread ASP.NET (old, System.Web) ✅ Yes — the request context ASP.NET Core ❌ No Console apps ❌ No

docs.title: The classic deadlock
docs.text:
// In a WinForms button handler, or old ASP.NET
public void Button_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    var data = GetDataAsync().Result;      // ← DEADLOCK
    label.Text = data;
}

private async Task<string> GetDataAsync()
{
    await Task.Delay(100);                 // continuation wants the UI thread
    return "done";
}

Step by step:

  1. Button_Click runs on the UI thread.
  2. .Result blocks the UI thread, waiting.
  3. Inside, await Task.Delay(100) captures the synchronization context.
  4. After 100 ms the delay finishes, and the continuation — return "done" — is posted to the UI thread.
  5. The UI thread is blocked at step 2 and cannot run it.
  6. The task never completes, so .Result never returns. Frozen forever.

The application hangs with no exception and no stack trace pointing anywhere useful.

docs.title: What ConfigureAwait(false) does
docs.text:
It says: "I do not need to resume on the original context. Any thread will do."

private async Task<string> GetDataAsync()
{
    await Task.Delay(100).ConfigureAwait(false);   // resume on a pool thread
    return "done";
}

Now the continuation runs on a thread-pool thread, the task completes, and .Result returns. The deadlock is gone.

But this is a workaround, not a fix. The real fix is not to block:

public async void Button_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)   // async void OK for handlers
{
    var data = await GetDataAsync();       // no blocking, no deadlock
    label.Text = data;
}

docs.title: ASP.NET Core: no deadlock, but still a serious problem
docs.text:
ASP.NET Core removed the synchronization context deliberately. So this does not deadlock:

public IActionResult Get()
{
    var data = _service.GetDataAsync().Result;   // no deadlock in ASP.NET Core
    return Ok(data);
}

It still must not be done. Here is why:

The whole point of async is that a thread is released while waiting (2.10). .Result throws that away — the thread sits blocked for the entire duration of the I/O.

Under load that becomes thread-pool starvation:

  1. 100 requests arrive, each blocking a pool thread on a 200 ms database call.
  2. All available pool threads are blocked. None can pick up new work.
  3. The pool does add threads — but slowly, roughly one or two per second by design.
  4. Meanwhile requests queue up. Latency goes from 200 ms to 30 seconds.
  5. Health checks time out. The orchestrator restarts the container. Traffic shifts to the remaining instances, which then fall over the same way.

The failure looks like a total outage, and CPU usage is near zero — because every thread is sitting doing nothing. That signature, high latency with idle CPU, is the classic fingerprint of this bug and a great thing to be able to name in an interview. See 19.12.

docs.title: So do you need ConfigureAwait(false) in ASP.NET Core?
docs.text:
Where Needed? Application code (controllers, services in your web app) No. There is no context to capture, so it changes nothing. Library code (a NuGet package, shared code) Yes. Your library might be consumed by a WinForms app that does have a context.

So in an ASP.NET Core project, adding .ConfigureAwait(false) everywhere is noise. In a reusable library, it is correct practice.

.NET 8 added ConfigureAwait(ConfigureAwaitOptions.SuppressThrowing) and other options, but the false/true distinction above is what gets asked about.

docs.title: The three ways this appears in real code
docs.text:
// 1. Blocking on a task
var user = _service.GetUserAsync(id).Result;
_service.SaveAsync(user).Wait();

// 2. Sync-over-async wrapper — a whole method that exists to block
public User GetUser(Guid id) => GetUserAsync(id).GetAwaiter().GetResult();

// 3. Blocking inside a constructor, because constructors cannot be async
public MyService()
{
    _config = LoadConfigAsync().Result;      // ← very common
}

docs.title: The fixes
docs.text:
// 1 & 2 — go async all the way up
public async Task<IActionResult> Get(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var user = await _service.GetUserAsync(id, ct);
    return Ok(user);
}

// 3 — constructors cannot be async, so do not do work in them.
// Use an async factory, or let DI resolve it.
public class MyService
{
    private Config? _config;

    private MyService() { }

    public static async Task<MyService> CreateAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var service = new MyService();
        service._config = await LoadConfigAsync(ct);
        return service;
    }
}

In ASP.NET Core specifically, the better answer for startup work is IHostedService or the options pattern — see 7.6 and 21.1.

docs.title: If you genuinely cannot avoid blocking
docs.text:
Sometimes you are in a legacy interface you cannot change. There is no safe answer, only a less unsafe one:

// Runs the async work on a fresh context-free thread, then blocks on that.
var result = Task.Run(() => GetDataAsync()).GetAwaiter().GetResult();

This avoids the deadlock because Task.Run moves the work off the captured context. It still blocks a thread. Treat it as a documented last resort, not a pattern.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why does calling .Result on a task sometimes deadlock?

Because the thread blocks waiting for the task, while the task's continuation is queued to run on that same blocked thread. In a UI application or old ASP.NET, await captures the synchronization context so the code after it resumes on the original thread. If that thread is blocked inside .Result, the continuation can never run, the task never completes, and the block never ends. It is effectively one thread waiting for itself.

Q: Does that happen in ASP.NET Core?

No, because ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context — continuations run on any available thread-pool thread, so there is nothing to deadlock against. But blocking is still a serious problem there for a different reason. It defeats the purpose of async by pinning a thread for the whole duration of the I/O, and under load that causes thread-pool starvation: all pool threads end up blocked, the pool only injects new ones at about one or two per second, and latency collapses. The distinctive symptom is very high latency with almost no CPU usage.

Q: What does ConfigureAwait(false) do, and do you need it?

It tells the runtime not to capture the current synchronization context, so the continuation can resume on any thread rather than being posted back to the original one. That is what prevents the classic deadlock. In ASP.NET Core application code it does nothing, because there is no context to capture, so adding it everywhere is just noise. It genuinely matters in library code, because you do not control who consumes your library — it might be a desktop app that does have a context, and without it your library could deadlock their application.

Q: How would you diagnose thread-pool starvation in production?

The signature is high request latency combined with low CPU — the threads are blocked, not busy. I would check the ThreadPool queue length and thread count via dotnet-counters, where you would see the queue growing and the thread count climbing slowly. Then I would take a dump with dotnet-dump and look at the stacks; starvation shows up as many threads all sitting in Monitor.Wait or Task.Result. The fix is to find the sync-over-async call and make the path async all the way up.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• .Result, .Wait(), and .GetAwaiter().GetResult() all block. All three are the same problem.
  • It works in development and fails in production. With one user there are plenty of free threads; the failure only appears under concurrency.
  • ConfigureAwait(false) in ASP.NET Core app code does nothing. It is not a fix for blocking, and it is not needed there.
  • In libraries, omitting ConfigureAwait(false) can deadlock your consumers.
  • Constructors cannot be async, which is why people block in them. Use an async factory instead.
  • .Result wraps exceptions in AggregateException, so your catch (SqlException) will not match. See 2.16.
  • One blocking call deep in a library can starve the whole application. The problem is not local to where it is written.

docs.title: 2.14 — CancellationToken and Cooperative Cancellation
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.13 Async deadlocks · Next: 2.15 async void

Markers: 🔥 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Cancellation in .NET is cooperative. Nothing is forcibly stopped — the token is a request, and your code has to check it.
  • Pass the token down through every async call. A token you accept and ignore is worse than useless, because it looks like cancellation works.
  • OperationCanceledException is a normal outcome, not an error. Do not log it as one.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
A user opens a page that runs a 30-second report, waits three seconds, and closes the tab. Without cancellation, your server keeps working for the remaining 27 seconds — running the query, building the result, serialising it — and then writes it to a connection that is already gone.

Multiply that by every impatient user and you are burning a significant fraction of your capacity on work nobody will ever see.

CancellationToken fixes that, but only cooperatively. There is no way to forcibly kill running code in .NET — an old method called Thread.Abort tried, and it was so dangerous (it could interrupt code mid-way through updating shared state) that it is removed entirely in modern .NET.

So cancellation works like tapping someone on the shoulder and saying "you can stop now." They have to notice, and they choose a sensible moment to stop. If they never look up, they carry on regardless.

docs.title: The two halves
docs.text:
// The SOURCE — the side that triggers cancellation
var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();

// The TOKEN — the side that observes it. Handed to the work.
CancellationToken token = cts.Token;

// Later, from anywhere:
cts.Cancel();

Keep the split clear: whoever starts the work holds the source; whoever does the work gets the token. Never pass the source down — that would let called code cancel its own caller.

docs.title: Three ways to observe it
docs.text:
// 1. Throw if cancelled — the usual choice
token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();

// 2. Check without throwing — for a clean partial exit
if (token.IsCancellationRequested)
    return partialResults;

// 3. Register a callback — for cleanup
token.Register(() => _logger.LogInformation("Cancelled, cleaning up"));

docs.title: Passing it down — the part that actually matters
docs.text:
public async Task<Report> BuildAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var orders = await _db.Orders
        .Where(o => o.CustomerId == id)
        .ToListAsync(ct);                     // ← pass it

    var rates = await _http.GetFromJsonAsync<Rates>("/rates", ct);   // ← and here

    foreach (var order in orders)
    {
        ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();    // ← check in long loops
        Process(order);
    }

    return new Report(orders, rates);
}

A token you accept and do not use is a lie. The signature promises cancellability and the implementation ignores it. This is extremely common in real code and worth checking for in a review.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
CancellationTokenSource has a built-in timer:

using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
await LongRunningAsync(cts.Token);       // throws after 30s

docs.title: Combining tokens
docs.text:
Very common in ASP.NET Core — you want "cancel if the client disconnects or if 30 seconds pass":

using var timeout = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
using var linked  = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(
    requestAborted, timeout.Token);

await DoWorkAsync(linked.Token);      // cancels on whichever fires first

⚠️ CreateLinkedTokenSource returns something you must dispose. Forgetting leaves the registration attached to the parent token, which leaks memory if the parent is long-lived. The using above is not optional.

docs.title: CancellationToken.None
docs.text:
For work that genuinely must not be interrupted:

await _audit.RecordAsync(entry, CancellationToken.None);

Use this deliberately, for things like writing an audit record after a state change — where stopping halfway would leave data inconsistent. Do not use it just to silence a compiler warning.

docs.title: In ASP.NET Core
docs.text:
The framework gives you a token automatically. Just add it as an action parameter:

[HttpGet("report/{id:guid}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> GetReport(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // Model binding supplies HttpContext.RequestAborted here automatically
    var report = await _service.BuildAsync(id, ct);
    return Ok(report);
}

That token is cancelled when the client disconnects. Adding the parameter costs one word and is the single easiest performance improvement available in most controllers.

docs.title: ⚠️ Do not log cancellation as an error
docs.text:
When a user navigates away, you get an OperationCanceledException. That is normal, not a failure:

// BAD — fills your error dashboards with noise
catch (Exception ex)
{
    _logger.LogError(ex, "Request failed");
}

// GOOD — treat cancellation as the routine event it is
catch (OperationCanceledException) when (ct.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    _logger.LogInformation("Request cancelled by client");
    // Do not return an error response — nobody is listening anyway
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    _logger.LogError(ex, "Request failed");
    throw;
}

Note the when (ct.IsCancellationRequested) filter. Without it you would also swallow cancellations caused by your own timeouts, which usually are worth reporting as an error. The filter distinguishes "the client left" from "our upstream call timed out".

TaskCanceledException inherits from OperationCanceledException, so catching the parent covers both.

docs.title: Background services
docs.text:
BackgroundService hands you a token that fires on shutdown. Honouring it is what makes graceful shutdown work:

protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        await ProcessBatchAsync(stoppingToken);
        await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), stoppingToken);
    }
}

If you ignore stoppingToken, the host waits for its shutdown timeout (5 seconds by default) and then kills the process mid-work. In Kubernetes that means dropped requests on every deployment. See 24.6.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic service that does it properly throughout:

public class ExportService(AppDbContext db, IFileStore store, ILogger<ExportService> log)
{
    public async Task<string> ExportAsync(Guid customerId, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // Our own limit, on top of whatever the caller passed
        using var timeout = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));
        using var linked  = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(ct, timeout.Token);
        var token = linked.Token;

        try
        {
            var orders = await db.Orders
                .Where(o => o.CustomerId == customerId)
                .AsNoTracking()
                .ToListAsync(token);

            var csv = new StringBuilder();
            foreach (var order in orders)
            {
                token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();     // check inside the loop
                csv.AppendLine($"{order.Id},{order.Total}");
            }

            // Deliberately NOT cancellable: a half-written file is worse
            // than a wasted one. Finish what we started.
            return await store.SaveAsync(csv.ToString(), CancellationToken.None);
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException) when (ct.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            log.LogInformation("Export cancelled by caller");
            throw;
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException)
        {
            // Our 5-minute limit fired — this IS worth reporting
            log.LogWarning("Export timed out after 5 minutes");
            throw new TimeoutException("Export took too long");
        }
    }
}

The three deliberate decisions there are all worth explaining in an interview:

  • Linked token so both the caller's cancellation and our own timeout work.
  • ThrowIfCancellationRequested inside the loop, because a long loop with no await has no other cancellation point.
  • CancellationToken.None for the file write, because a partially written file is worse than doing unnecessary work.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is a CancellationToken and how does cancellation work in .NET?

Cancellation is cooperative — nothing is forcibly stopped. A CancellationTokenSource is held by whoever starts the work, and it hands out a CancellationToken that gets passed down into the work. When the source is cancelled, the token's flag flips, and it is up to the code doing the work to notice — either by calling ThrowIfCancellationRequested, by checking IsCancellationRequested, or by passing the token to a framework method that checks it. If nobody checks, nothing stops. There is no forcible abort in modern .NET, because the old Thread.Abort could interrupt code halfway through mutating shared state and was removed.

Q: Where does the token come from in an ASP.NET Core controller?

You add a CancellationToken parameter to the action and model binding supplies HttpContext.RequestAborted automatically. It fires when the client disconnects, so passing it into your database calls and HTTP calls means the server stops working on responses nobody will receive. It costs one parameter and is probably the cheapest throughput improvement available in a typical controller.

Q: How should you handle OperationCanceledException?

Treat it as a normal outcome rather than an error. If a user navigates away mid-request you will get one, and logging it at error level fills your dashboards with noise that hides real failures. I catch it with a filter checking whether the caller's token was the one cancelled — if so I log at information level, and if not it means our own timeout fired, which is genuinely worth a warning or converting into a TimeoutException. Worth knowing that TaskCanceledException derives from it, so catching the base type covers both.

Q: What is a linked token source for?

Combining several cancellation reasons into one token — typically "cancel if the client disconnects, or if our own timeout expires". CreateLinkedTokenSource gives you a token that fires when any of its parents fire. The important detail is that it is disposable and you must dispose it, because it registers callbacks on the parent tokens; if the parent is long-lived and you forget, those registrations accumulate and leak.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Accepting a token and not using it. The signature promises cancellability that does not exist. Very common.
  • Not passing the token to nested calls. Cancellation stops at the first method that drops it.
  • Logging OperationCanceledException as an error. It is routine traffic.
  • Forgetting to dispose a linked token source. It leaks registrations on the parent.
  • A long CPU loop with no await has no cancellation point. You must call ThrowIfCancellationRequested explicitly.
  • Ignoring stoppingToken in a BackgroundService breaks graceful shutdown and drops work on every deployment.
  • Cancelling work that must complete can corrupt state. Use CancellationToken.None deliberately for audit writes and similar.
  • cts.Cancel() runs registered callbacks synchronously on the cancelling thread. A slow callback blocks whoever called Cancel.

docs.title: 2.15 — async void: Why It Is Almost Always Wrong
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.14 CancellationToken · Next: 2.16 Async exceptions

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• You cannot await an async void method. The caller has no way to know when it finished, or whether it worked.
  • An exception inside it cannot be caught by the caller. It goes straight to the top and crashes the process.
  • The only acceptable use is a UI event handler, where the signature is forced on you — and even then it needs a try/catch around the whole body.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
An async method can return three things: Task, Task<T>, or void.

The first two hand back an object representing the operation — so the caller can wait for it, check whether it failed, and get a result. async void hands back nothing.

A picture: async Task is posting a letter with tracking. async void is shouting into a corridor and walking away.

With tracking, you know when it arrived and if it went wrong. Shouting into a corridor gives you nothing — you do not know if anyone heard, when they heard, or whether they fell over trying to act on it.

That missing return value causes two separate serious problems, and the exception one is genuinely dangerous.

docs.title: Problem 1: you cannot await it
docs.text:
public async void SaveData() { await _db.SaveChangesAsync(); }

public void Caller()
{
    SaveData();                       // returns IMMEDIATELY, work still running
    Console.WriteLine("Saved!");      // prints before the save has finished

    // There is no way to wait. Nothing was returned to wait ON.
}

The method returns at its first await, exactly as 2.11 describes — but with no Task handed back, the caller has no handle on it. The work continues invisibly, in the background, unobserved.

This creates race conditions that are maddening to debug, because the code looks sequential.

docs.title: Problem 2: exceptions crash the process ⚠️
docs.text:
This is the serious one.

public async void ProcessAsync()
{
    throw new InvalidOperationException("boom");
}

public void Caller()
{
    try
    {
        ProcessAsync();               // the try/catch does NOTHING
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        // NEVER REACHED
        Console.WriteLine("caught it");
    }
}

Why does the catch not work? Because by the time the exception is thrown, ProcessAsync has already returned to the caller — the try block finished. The exception happens later, on whatever thread the continuation runs on.

With async Task, the exception is captured and stored inside the returned Task, so awaiting it rethrows and your catch works.

With async void there is no Task to store it in. So the runtime raises it on the synchronization context, or if there is none, on the thread pool as an unhandled exception — which terminates the process.

// In ASP.NET Core: this brings down your entire application
public async void FireAndForget()
{
    await Task.Delay(100);
    throw new Exception("boom");     // → process crash. Every in-flight request lost.
}

Not a 500 response. Not a logged error. The whole worker process dies, taking every concurrent request with it. In Kubernetes the container restarts and traffic shifts, and if the bug is triggered by normal traffic it will happen again immediately.

docs.title: The one legitimate use
docs.text:
Event handlers, where the delegate signature is fixed and you cannot return a Task:

private async void Button_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    // 'async void' is forced here — EventHandler returns void
}

And even then, wrap the entire body in a try/catch, because nothing else can:

private async void Button_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    try
    {
        await DoWorkAsync();
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        _logger.LogError(ex, "Button click failed");
        MessageBox.Show("Something went wrong");
    }
}

Better still, keep the handler as a thin shell over a testable async Task method:

private async void Button_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    try { await HandleClickAsync(); }
    catch (Exception ex) { _logger.LogError(ex, "failed"); }
}

private async Task HandleClickAsync()      // testable, awaitable
{
    await DoWorkAsync();
}

docs.title: The trap you will actually hit
docs.text:
async void rarely gets written on purpose. It usually appears by accident, through a lambda passed to a method expecting Action:

// Looks fine. Is async void.
timer.Elapsed += async (s, e) => await DoWorkAsync();

// Also async void — Action returns void
_items.ForEach(async item => await ProcessAsync(item));

// Also async void
Parallel.ForEach(items, async item => await ProcessAsync(item));

The last two are especially nasty. List<T>.ForEach takes an Action<T>, so your async lambda becomes async void. The loop finishes instantly with every operation still running, ForEach returns, and the caller carries on thinking the work is done. Any exception crashes the process.

The fix is an ordinary foreach, or Task.WhenAll:

// Sequential, awaited properly
foreach (var item in items)
    await ProcessAsync(item);

// Or concurrent — see 2.12
await Task.WhenAll(items.Select(item => ProcessAsync(item)));

How to spot it: if you write async on a lambda, check what delegate type it is being assigned to. Action means async void. Func<Task> is fine.

docs.title: Fire-and-forget done properly
docs.text:
Sometimes you genuinely want to start work and not wait — logging telemetry, say. async void is still the wrong tool:

// WRONG
async void SendTelemetry() { await _client.SendAsync(data); }

// Better — at least the exception is caught rather than crashing
_ = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    try { await _client.SendAsync(data); }
    catch (Exception ex) { _logger.LogError(ex, "Telemetry failed"); }
});

But in ASP.NET Core, do not do either. Work started this way dies when the request ends or when the app shuts down, so it silently disappears. Use a proper background mechanism — IHostedService, a Channel, or a real queue. See 21.1.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The full comparison:

// ✗ async void — unawaitable, uncatchable, crashes on failure
public async void SaveAsync(Order o) => await _db.SaveAsync(o);

// ✓ async Task — awaitable, exceptions captured in the task
public async Task SaveAsync(Order o) => await _db.SaveAsync(o);

// ✗ accidental async void via Action<T>
orders.ForEach(async o => await SaveAsync(o));

// ✓ sequential
foreach (var o in orders)
    await SaveAsync(o);

// ✓ concurrent
await Task.WhenAll(orders.Select(SaveAsync));

// ✓ the ONLY good async void — an event handler, fully guarded
private async void OnTimerElapsed(object? sender, ElapsedEventArgs e)
{
    try
    {
        await _processor.RunAsync(_cts.Token);
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException)
    {
        // shutting down — normal
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        _logger.LogError(ex, "Timer processing failed");
        // MUST swallow here. Rethrowing crashes the process.
    }
}

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why is async void bad?

Two reasons, and the second is severe. First, it returns nothing, so the caller cannot await it — there is no way to know when the work finished or whether it succeeded, which produces race conditions in code that looks sequential. Second, exceptions cannot be caught by the caller. With async Task the exception is captured inside the returned task and rethrown when you await it. With async void there is no task to store it in, so it is raised as an unhandled exception on the thread pool, which terminates the process. In ASP.NET Core that means the whole application goes down and every in-flight request is lost.

Q: When is async void acceptable?

Only for event handlers, where the delegate signature is fixed as returning void and you have no choice. Even then the entire body needs a try/catch, because that is the only place the exception can possibly be handled. My preference is to keep the handler as a thin wrapper — try/catch around a call to a proper async Task method that holds the real logic, so the logic stays testable and awaitable.

Q: How does async void usually get into a codebase?

Almost never deliberately. It slips in through lambdas passed to methods that expect an Action — List<T>.ForEach, Parallel.ForEach, timer event subscriptions. Writing items.ForEach(async x => await ProcessAsync(x)) looks like it awaits each item, but ForEach takes an Action<T>, so every lambda is async void. The loop completes instantly with all the work still running unobserved, and any failure crashes the process. The habit is to check what delegate type an async lambda is being assigned to — Func<Task> is fine, Action is not.

Q: How do you do fire-and-forget properly?

In a web application, you usually should not. Work started during a request dies when the request or the process ends, so it silently disappears — and there is no retry and no visibility. The right answer is a proper background mechanism: an IHostedService or BackgroundService reading from a Channel, or a real message queue if the work must survive a restart. If I truly needed fire-and-forget for something disposable like telemetry, I would at least use Task.Run with a try/catch inside so a failure is logged rather than fatal.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• A try/catch around an async void call catches nothing. The method already returned.
  • An unhandled exception in async void terminates the process. Not a 500 — a crash.
  • List<T>.ForEach with an async lambda is async void. So is Parallel.ForEach. Use foreach or Task.WhenAll.
  • Timer and event subscriptions with async lambdas are async void by definition.
  • async void cannot be tested. There is nothing to await, so a test finishes before the work does.
  • Fire-and-forget in ASP.NET Core silently dies on request end or shutdown.
  • The compiler does not warn you. async void is legal C# and looks intentional.

docs.title: 2.16 — Exceptions in Async Code, AggregateException
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.15 async void · Next: 2.17 IAsyncEnumerable

Markers: ⭐ ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• An exception in an async Task method is stored inside the returned Task, not thrown immediately. It surfaces when you await.
  • await unwraps it, so you catch the real exception type. .Result does not — you get an AggregateException wrapper instead, and your catch (SqlException) will not match.
  • With Task.WhenAll, awaiting rethrows only the first exception. The others are still on the task.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
In normal synchronous code, an exception travels straight up the call stack until something catches it.

Async breaks that, because the method returns before it finishes (2.11). By the time the failure happens, the caller has already moved on — there is no stack to travel up any more.

So the runtime does something different: it puts the exception in a box — the Task — and hands the box back. The exception sits there quietly until someone opens the box by awaiting it. At that moment it is thrown, on the caller's behalf.

A picture: a parcel with something broken inside. The courier does not tell you at the door. You find out when you open it. If you never open it, you never find out — which is the "unobserved exception" problem later in this note.

docs.title: The exception is stored, not thrown
docs.text:
public async Task<int> FailAsync()
{
    await Task.Delay(10);
    throw new InvalidOperationException("boom");
}

var task = FailAsync();          // NO exception here — the task is just faulted
Console.WriteLine("still running");

await task;                      // exception thrown HERE

The task has three possible end states: RanToCompletion, Faulted, or Canceled. Awaiting a faulted task rethrows what is inside it.

docs.title: await unwraps; .Result does not ⚠️
docs.text:
This is the practical difference that bites people.

// With await — you catch the REAL exception type
try
{
    await GetDataAsync();
}
catch (SqlException ex)          // ✓ matches
{
    _logger.LogError(ex, "Database failed");
}

// With .Result — wrapped in AggregateException
try
{
    var data = GetDataAsync().Result;
}
catch (SqlException ex)          // ✗ NEVER MATCHES
{
    // The thrown type is AggregateException, which WRAPS the SqlException.
    // This catch block is dead code.
}

To handle it you would need:

catch (AggregateException ex) when (ex.InnerException is SqlException sql)
{
    _logger.LogError(sql, "Database failed");
}

Which is a strong argument for never blocking in the first place — see 2.13. await gives you clean, expected exception types.

GetAwaiter().GetResult() does unwrap correctly, unlike .Result — but it still blocks a thread, so it is not a fix.

docs.title: Task.WhenAll and multiple failures
docs.text:
var t1 = FailAsync("first");
var t2 = FailAsync("second");
var t3 = FailAsync("third");

var all = Task.WhenAll(t1, t2, t3);

try
{
    await all;
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    // ex is ONLY the first exception. The other two are invisible here.
    _logger.LogError(ex, "Something failed");
}

To see all of them, go to the task itself:

try
{
    await all;
}
catch
{
    foreach (var inner in all.Exception!.InnerExceptions)
        _logger.LogError(inner, "Task failed");
}

all.Exception is always an AggregateException containing every failure. Awaiting only surfaced the first, which is convenient for the common case and misleading when several fail at once.

docs.title: Where try/catch goes
docs.text:
A try/catch around an await works exactly as you would expect:

public async Task ProcessAsync()
{
    try
    {
        await _db.SaveAsync();       // ✓ caught normally
    }
    catch (DbUpdateException ex)
    {
        _logger.LogError(ex, "Save failed");
    }
}

The state machine restores the try/catch context when it resumes, so exceptions after an await are caught by a catch written before it. That is one of the nicer things the compiler does for you.

But a try/catch around a call without an await does not:

try
{
    var task = ProcessAsync();       // no await — exception goes into the task
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    // NOT reached. Nothing was thrown here.
}

docs.title: Cancellation is not a failure
docs.text:
OperationCanceledException is thrown by cancellation and puts the task in the Canceled state, not Faulted. Treat it separately:

try
{
    await DoWorkAsync(ct);
}
catch (OperationCanceledException) when (ct.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    _logger.LogInformation("Cancelled");     // routine — not an error
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    _logger.LogError(ex, "Actually failed");
    throw;
}

See 2.14 for why the when filter matters.

docs.title: Unobserved exceptions
docs.text:
If a task faults and nobody ever awaits it, the exception is never observed:

_ = SaveAsync();       // fire and forget — if this fails, nobody hears

In .NET Framework this crashed the process when the task was garbage collected. Modern .NET changed the default so it does not — which is safer, but means the failure is now completely silent. Arguably worse for debugging.

You can hook the event to at least log them:

TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException += (sender, e) =>
{
    _logger.LogError(e.Exception, "Unobserved task exception");
    e.SetObserved();
};

That is a safety net for diagnostics, not a substitute for awaiting your tasks.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Realistic handling of a set of parallel operations where partial failure is expected:

public async Task<ImportResult> ImportAllAsync(
    IReadOnlyList<string> files,
    CancellationToken ct)
{
    // Each task captures its own outcome rather than throwing outward,
    // so one bad file does not abandon the rest.
    var tasks = files.Select(async file =>
    {
        try
        {
            var count = await ImportFileAsync(file, ct);
            return new FileOutcome(file, count, Error: null);
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException)
        {
            throw;                              // cancellation must propagate
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            _logger.LogWarning(ex, "Failed to import {File}", file);
            return new FileOutcome(file, 0, Error: ex.Message);
        }
    });

    var outcomes = await Task.WhenAll(tasks);   // no exception — all handled inside

    return new ImportResult(
        Succeeded: outcomes.Where(o => o.Error is null).ToList(),
        Failed:    outcomes.Where(o => o.Error is not null).ToList());
}

The pattern here — catch inside each task and return a result object — is worth knowing. It avoids WhenAll hiding all but the first exception, and it means one failure does not discard the work that succeeded.

Note that OperationCanceledException is deliberately rethrown. If the whole operation is being cancelled, you do not want to record that as "this file failed".

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What happens to an exception thrown inside an async Task method?

It is not thrown to the caller immediately, because the method has usually already returned at its first await. Instead the runtime captures it and stores it on the returned Task, putting that task into the Faulted state. The exception surfaces when someone awaits the task, at which point it is rethrown on the awaiting code. If nobody ever awaits it, the exception is never observed — in modern .NET that no longer crashes the process, but it does mean the failure is completely silent.

Q: Why does catch (SqlException) sometimes not catch a database error in async code?

Because of how you awaited it. await unwraps the stored exception and rethrows the original type, so a typed catch works. But .Result and .Wait() throw an AggregateException that wraps the real one, so a catch (SqlException) never matches and the block is effectively dead code. That is one more reason not to block on tasks — beyond the thread cost, it changes the exception type you have to handle.

Q: If several tasks in a Task.WhenAll fail, what do you get?

Awaiting the combined task rethrows only the first exception, which is easy to mistake for "only one thing went wrong". All of them are recorded on the task itself — task.Exception is an AggregateException whose InnerExceptions collection holds every failure. So if I need to log or report all of them, I keep a reference to the combined task and inspect that in the catch block rather than relying on what await threw.

Q: How would you handle a batch of operations where some are expected to fail?

I would catch inside each individual task and return a result object describing success or failure, rather than letting exceptions escape to WhenAll. That way one bad item does not hide the others behind a single rethrown exception, and it does not discard the work that succeeded. The one exception I would deliberately let propagate is OperationCanceledException, because that means the whole operation is being torn down rather than that one item failed.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• .Result and .Wait() wrap the exception in AggregateException. Typed catch blocks silently stop matching.
  • Task.WhenAll rethrows only the first exception. Check task.Exception.InnerExceptions for the rest.
  • A try/catch around a call you did not await catches nothing. The exception went into the task.
  • An unobserved faulted task is silent in modern .NET. No crash, no log, nothing.
  • OperationCanceledException is not a fault. Handle it separately or you will log routine cancellations as errors.
  • An exception in async void cannot be caught at all and crashes the process. See 2.15.
  • throw inside a catch in an async method preserves the stack correctly, but throw ex still resets it, exactly as in sync code. See 1.20.

docs.title: 2.17 — IAsyncEnumerable and await foreach
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.16 Async exceptions · Next: 2.18 Thread safety

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• IAsyncEnumerable<T> is IEnumerable<T> where getting the next item is itself awaitable.
  • It solves a real gap: Task<List<T>> gives you everything at once, and IEnumerable<T> cannot await. Async streams give you items one at a time, as they arrive.
  • Consume it with await foreach. Pass cancellation with [EnumeratorCancellation].

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Before C# 8 there were two options for returning a sequence from an async method, and both had a flaw:

Task<List<Order>> GetOrdersAsync();   // must build the WHOLE list before returning
IEnumerable<Order> GetOrders();       // streams one at a time, but cannot await

The first loses streaming — a million rows means a million objects in memory before the caller sees one. The second cannot do async I/O, so it blocks a thread on every read.

IAsyncEnumerable<T> gives you both: stream one item at a time, and await between items.

A picture: a conveyor belt from a warehouse rather than a delivery van. The van (Task<List<T>>) turns up once with everything, and you wait for the whole load. The belt delivers items as they are picked, you start working on the first one immediately, and you can stop the belt whenever you have enough.

docs.title: Producing one
docs.text:
Same as a normal iterator (2.4), but async with IAsyncEnumerable<T>:

public async IAsyncEnumerable<Order> StreamOrdersAsync(
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    await using var connection = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
    await connection.OpenAsync(ct);

    await using var command = new SqlCommand("SELECT * FROM Orders", connection);
    await using var reader = await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(ct);

    while (await reader.ReadAsync(ct))          // await INSIDE the iterator
    {
        yield return new Order
        {
            Id    = reader.GetGuid(0),
            Total = reader.GetDecimal(1)
        };
    }
}

Note there is no return type of Task — it is async IAsyncEnumerable<T>, and you still use yield return. The compiler builds an async state machine that also implements IAsyncEnumerator<T>.

docs.title: Consuming one
docs.text:
await foreach (var order in StreamOrdersAsync(ct))
{
    Console.WriteLine(order.Total);
}

await foreach calls MoveNextAsync() — which returns a ValueTask<bool> — and awaits it before each item.

docs.title: [EnumeratorCancellation] — the bit people get wrong
docs.text:
Look again at that parameter attribute. Without it, cancellation silently does nothing.

The problem: await foreach can supply its own token via WithCancellation(...), and the method also has a ct parameter. Which one wins?

// The consumer supplies a token here
await foreach (var o in StreamOrdersAsync().WithCancellation(ct))

[EnumeratorCancellation] tells the compiler "wire the token from WithCancellation into this parameter". Without the attribute, ct stays at its default value of None and cancellation is ignored entirely — with no warning.

So the two ways to cancel are:

// Pass it directly as an argument
await foreach (var o in StreamOrdersAsync(ct)) { }

// Or via WithCancellation — needs [EnumeratorCancellation] to work
await foreach (var o in StreamOrdersAsync().WithCancellation(ct)) { }

Always add the attribute. It costs nothing and makes both forms work.

docs.title: LINQ over async streams
docs.text:
The standard LINQ operators do not work on IAsyncEnumerable<T> — they are built for IEnumerable<T>. You need the System.Linq.Async NuGet package:

var expensive = await StreamOrdersAsync(ct)
    .Where(o => o.Total > 1000)
    .Take(10)
    .ToListAsync(ct);

.NET 10 began bringing some of these into the base library, but for now the package is the usual answer.

docs.title: Where it earns its place in ASP.NET Core
Streaming a large API response
docs.text:
[HttpGet("orders/stream")]
public async IAsyncEnumerable<OrderDto> Stream(
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct)
{
    await foreach (var order in _repo.StreamAllAsync(ct))
        yield return _mapper.ToDto(order);
}

ASP.NET Core understands IAsyncEnumerable<T> return types natively. It serialises items to the response as they are produced, so:

  • Memory stays flat regardless of how many rows there are.
  • The client starts receiving data almost immediately rather than after the full query.
  • If the client disconnects, ct fires and the query stops.

Compare with returning Task<List<OrderDto>> for a million rows: a million DTOs in memory, one enormous JSON string built in memory, and nothing sent until it is all ready.

docs.title: EF Core
docs.text:
AsAsyncEnumerable() streams rows instead of buffering them:

await foreach (var order in _db.Orders.AsAsyncEnumerable().WithCancellation(ct))
{
    await ProcessAsync(order, ct);
}

⚠️ The database connection stays open for the whole loop. If processing each item is slow, you are holding a connection from the pool for a long time. For heavy per-item work, read in batches instead:

const int BatchSize = 500;
var skip = 0;

while (true)
{
    var batch = await _db.Orders.OrderBy(o => o.Id)
        .Skip(skip).Take(BatchSize).ToListAsync(ct);

    if (batch.Count == 0) break;

    foreach (var order in batch)
        await ProcessAsync(order, ct);      // connection already released

    skip += BatchSize;
}

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Reading a huge file line by line without loading it, and without blocking:

public async IAsyncEnumerable<LogEntry> ParseLogAsync(
    string path,
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    using var reader = new StreamReader(path);

    while (await reader.ReadLineAsync(ct) is { } line)     // pattern match: not null
    {
        if (TryParse(line, out var entry))
            yield return entry;
    }
}

Used with early exit:

await foreach (var entry in ParseLogAsync("huge.log", ct))
{
    if (entry.Level == LogLevel.Error)
    {
        _logger.LogWarning("First error at {Time}", entry.Timestamp);
        break;               // stops reading — the file reader is disposed properly
    }
}

A 10 GB file where the first error is on line 40 reads 40 lines. Memory stays at one line. And because break disposes the enumerator, the using inside the iterator runs and the file handle closes.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is IAsyncEnumerable<T> and what problem does it solve?

It is a sequence where fetching each item is itself asynchronous. Before it existed you had to choose between Task<List<T>>, which forces you to build the entire collection before returning anything, and IEnumerable<T>, which streams but cannot await — so any I/O inside it blocks a thread. Async streams give you both: items are produced one at a time as they become available, and the producer can await between them. You consume it with await foreach.

Q: What does [EnumeratorCancellation] do?

It connects the token supplied by the consumer through WithCancellation to the CancellationToken parameter of your iterator method. Without the attribute, that parameter just keeps its default value of CancellationToken.None, so cancellation silently does nothing — the compiler has no way to know which parameter should receive the consumer's token. It is easy to miss because there is no error, just cancellation that quietly fails to work.

Q: When would you use it in ASP.NET Core?

Mainly for streaming large responses. ASP.NET Core supports returning IAsyncEnumerable<T> directly from an action and serialises items as they are produced, so memory stays flat and the client starts receiving data immediately rather than after the whole result set is built. For a query returning hundreds of thousands of rows that is the difference between a predictable memory profile and an out-of-memory exception. It is also useful for background processing pipelines where you want to start work on early items while later ones are still being fetched.

Q: What is the catch with AsAsyncEnumerable in EF Core?

The database connection stays open for the entire duration of the loop, because rows are being streamed as you consume them. If the work you do per item is slow, you are holding a pooled connection for a long time, and under load that can exhaust the pool. For lightweight per-item work it is fine; for anything heavy I would read in batches with Skip and Take instead, so the connection is released between batches.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Forgetting [EnumeratorCancellation] means cancellation silently does nothing.
  • Standard LINQ does not work on IAsyncEnumerable<T>. You need the System.Linq.Async package.
  • AsAsyncEnumerable holds a database connection for the whole loop. Batch instead if per-item work is slow.
  • You cannot use await foreach in a non-async method. The whole call chain must be async.
  • Enumerating twice runs the source twice, exactly as with IEnumerable. See 2.6.
  • Returning IAsyncEnumerable<T> from a controller means you cannot easily set a status code partway through — the response has already started once the first item is written.
  • Exceptions thrown mid-stream in a controller action arrive after headers are sent, so the client gets a truncated response rather than a clean error.
