docs.title: 2.18 — Thread Safety: lock, SemaphoreSlim, Interlocked, volatile
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.17 IAsyncEnumerable · Next: 2.19 Parallel programming

Markers: ⭐ ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• lock is the default tool. Simple, fast, and covers most cases — but you cannot await inside it.
  • SemaphoreSlim is the async-friendly alternative, because it has WaitAsync.
  • Interlocked does simple numeric operations atomically with no lock at all — much faster when it fits.
  • The real answer in ASP.NET Core is usually do not share mutable state at all.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
count++ looks like one instruction. It is three:

  1. Read the current value from memory
  2. Add one to it
  3. Write the result back

Two threads running that at the same time can interleave:

Thread A Thread B count 1 reads 5 5 2 reads 5 5 3 computes 6 5 4 computes 6 5 5 writes 6 6 6 writes 6 6

Two increments, one result. That is a race condition — the outcome depends on timing, so it works in testing and fails occasionally under load.

The picture: two people updating the same paper tally. Both read "5", both cross it out and write "6". One increment is silently lost. The fix is that only one person may hold the pen at a time.

docs.title: lock — one thread at a time
docs.text:
private readonly object _gate = new();
private int _count;

public void Increment()
{
    lock (_gate)          // only one thread inside this block at any moment
    {
        _count++;
    }
}

Rules that matter:

lock (this)              // ✗ BAD — external code can lock on your instance too
lock (typeof(MyClass))   // ✗ BAD — shared across the whole app domain
lock ("some string")     // ✗ BAD — string literals are interned and shared
lock (_gate)             // ✓ a private readonly object, used only for this

Always lock on a private readonly object that exists only to be a lock. Locking on anything publicly reachable means unrelated code can deadlock you.

.NET 9 added a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type which is faster and clearer:

private readonly Lock _gate = new();     // .NET 9+

docs.title: ⚠️ You cannot await inside a lock
docs.text:
lock (_gate)
{
    await SaveAsync();      // COMPILE ERROR
}

The compiler blocks it, and rightly so. A lock is tied to a specific thread — it must be released by the same thread that took it. After an await, your code may resume on a different thread, which could not release the lock. Deadlock.

docs.title: SemaphoreSlim — the async-safe lock
docs.text:
private readonly SemaphoreSlim _gate = new(1, 1);   // 1 = acts like a lock

public async Task UpdateAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await _gate.WaitAsync(ct);
    try
    {
        await _db.SaveAsync(order, ct);      // await IS allowed here
    }
    finally
    {
        _gate.Release();                     // MUST be in finally
    }
}

The (1, 1) means "initially 1 slot free, maximum 1 slot" — so it behaves like a mutex. Larger numbers make it a throttle:

private readonly SemaphoreSlim _throttle = new(10, 10);   // max 10 at once

The finally is not optional. If an exception escapes without releasing, that slot is gone forever and every future caller blocks. That is a total, permanent hang — a genuinely nasty production bug.

docs.title: Interlocked — atomic without locking
docs.text:
For simple numeric updates, the CPU can do it in one instruction:

private int _count;

Interlocked.Increment(ref _count);          // ++ atomically
Interlocked.Decrement(ref _count);
Interlocked.Add(ref _count, 5);
Interlocked.Exchange(ref _count, 0);        // set, returning the old value

// Set only if it currently equals the expected value
Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref _count, newValue, expectedValue);

Much faster than a lock — no blocking, no context switches. Use it whenever your shared state is a single number or reference. It cannot help with anything more complex.

docs.title: volatile — usually not what you want
docs.text:
volatile prevents the compiler and CPU from caching or reordering reads of a field:

private volatile bool _stopping;

// Thread A
_stopping = true;

// Thread B
while (!_stopping) { DoWork(); }    // without volatile, may never see the change

Without volatile, the JIT may hoist _stopping into a register and loop forever on a stale value.

But volatile does not make operations atomic. _count++ on a volatile field is still three steps and still races.

In practice you rarely want it. For a stop flag, use CancellationToken (2.14). For counters, use Interlocked. volatile is for lock-free algorithms, which almost nobody should be writing.

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text: Situation Use Simple counter or flag swap Interlocked Short synchronous critical section lock Critical section containing await SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync Limiting concurrency to N SemaphoreSlim(n, n) Shared collection A concurrent collection (2.3) Anything else Restructure so nothing is shared

docs.title: The best answer: do not share
docs.text:
In ASP.NET Core, most thread-safety problems come from state that should never have been shared. The framework already gives you the tools to avoid it:

// PROBLEM — a singleton holding mutable state needs locking everywhere
public class OrderService
{
    private List<Order> _pending = new();     // shared across ALL requests
}

// SOLUTION — scoped lifetime means one instance per request.
// No sharing, so no locking needed at all.
builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>();

Scoped services are the answer to most of this. Each request gets its own instance, so there is nothing to race over. Reserve singletons for things that are genuinely stateless or genuinely designed for concurrency. See 6.3.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A rate limiter using SemaphoreSlim as a throttle:

public class ApiClient(HttpClient http) : IDisposable
{
    // Allow at most 5 concurrent outbound calls
    private readonly SemaphoreSlim _throttle = new(5, 5);

    public async Task<T?> GetAsync<T>(string url, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await _throttle.WaitAsync(ct);
        try
        {
            return await http.GetFromJsonAsync<T>(url, ct);
        }
        finally
        {
            _throttle.Release();      // ALWAYS, even on exception or cancellation
        }
    }

    public void Dispose() => _throttle.Dispose();
}

And the Interlocked version of a metrics counter, which needs no lock at all:

public class RequestCounter
{
    private long _total;
    private long _failed;

    public void RecordSuccess() => Interlocked.Increment(ref _total);

    public void RecordFailure()
    {
        Interlocked.Increment(ref _total);
        Interlocked.Increment(ref _failed);
    }

    // Reading a long is NOT atomic on 32-bit systems, so read it properly
    public (long Total, long Failed) Snapshot() =>
        (Interlocked.Read(ref _total), Interlocked.Read(ref _failed));
}

⚠️ Note that the two increments in RecordFailure are individually atomic but not atomic together — a reader could see _total updated and _failed not yet. For metrics that is acceptable. If it were not, you would need a lock.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why is count++ not thread-safe?

Because it is three separate operations: read the value, add one, write it back. Two threads can both read the same starting value before either writes, so both compute the same result and one increment is lost. The failure depends entirely on timing, which is why it passes tests and fails intermittently under production load. Interlocked.Increment fixes it by doing the whole read-modify-write as a single atomic CPU instruction.

Q: Why can't you await inside a lock?

Because a lock has thread affinity — it must be released by the same thread that acquired it. After an await, the continuation can resume on a completely different thread, which would then try to release a lock it does not own. The compiler rejects it outright rather than letting you create that deadlock. When you need mutual exclusion around async work you use SemaphoreSlim with WaitAsync, because a semaphore is not tied to a thread.

Q: What should you lock on?

A private readonly object that exists solely as a lock. Locking on this, on a type, or on a string literal is dangerous because those are all reachable from outside your class — other code can take the same lock and deadlock you in ways that are extremely hard to trace. String literals are especially bad because they are interned, so two unrelated classes locking on the same literal share a lock. In .NET 9 there is a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type which is both clearer and faster.

Q: What is the best way to handle shared state in ASP.NET Core?

Usually to not have any. Most thread-safety problems there come from putting mutable state in a singleton, which is then shared across every concurrent request. Registering the service as scoped gives each request its own instance and the problem disappears entirely — no locks, no races, nothing to reason about. I would only reach for synchronisation primitives when state genuinely must be shared, like a cache or a counter, and even then a ConcurrentDictionary or Interlocked usually beats a hand-written lock.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Locking on this, a type, or a string literal. All publicly reachable, all can deadlock you from outside.
  • Forgetting Release() in a finally. One leaked semaphore slot hangs every future caller permanently.
  • volatile does not make operations atomic. It only prevents caching and reordering.
  • Two atomic operations are not atomic together. A reader can see a half-updated pair.
  • Holding a lock while doing I/O serialises your whole application on that call.
  • Nested locks in different orders deadlock. Always take locks in a consistent order.
  • lock in an async method is a compile error — but Monitor.Enter around an await is not, and it is a real deadlock. Do not work around the compiler.
  • long reads and writes are not atomic on 32-bit platforms. Use Interlocked.Read.

docs.title: 2.19 — Parallel.For, PLINQ, and When Not to Use Them
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.18 Thread safety · Next: 3.1 .NET history

Markers: ⭐ ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Parallel ≠ async. Parallel means "use many CPU cores on one job". Async means "do not block a thread while waiting".
  • Parallel.For and PLINQ are for CPU-bound work over lots of items. They are almost always wrong for I/O.
  • In ASP.NET Core they are usually a mistake, because the server is already busy running other requests in parallel.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
These two words get confused constantly, and the distinction is the point of this note.

Async is about waiting efficiently. Your code asks the network for something and gets on with other work instead of standing idle. It does not make anything faster — it stops threads being wasted.

Parallel is about working faster. You split a computation across CPU cores so it finishes sooner. It genuinely reduces wall-clock time, but only for work that actually uses the CPU.

A picture: one cook waiting for a pot to boil versus four cooks chopping vegetables.

The waiting cook should go and do something else meanwhile — that is async. It does not matter how many cooks you have; the pot boils at its own pace. But chopping a mountain of vegetables genuinely goes four times faster with four cooks — that is parallelism.

Using parallelism for waiting is like hiring four cooks to stand and watch the same pot.

docs.title: Parallel.For and Parallel.ForEach
docs.text:
// Sequential — one core
foreach (var image in images)
    Resize(image);

// Parallel — all available cores
Parallel.ForEach(images, image => Resize(image));

The runtime splits the collection across threads and manages the work. For genuinely CPU-heavy work over many items, this scales close to linearly with core count.

Controlling how many run at once:

Parallel.ForEach(
    images,
    new ParallelOptions
    {
        MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 4,
        CancellationToken = ct
    },
    image => Resize(image));

docs.title: Parallel.ForEachAsync (.NET 6+)
docs.text:
This one is genuinely useful, and it is the exception to "parallel is not for I/O". It runs async operations with a concurrency limit:

await Parallel.ForEachAsync(
    urls,
    new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 10, CancellationToken = ct },
    async (url, token) =>
    {
        var data = await http.GetStringAsync(url, token);
        await SaveAsync(data, token);
    });

This is the clean solution to the throttling problem from 2.12 — instead of SemaphoreSlim wrapped around a WhenAll, you get a built-in concurrency cap. Prefer this for "call a service for each of these 1,000 items, but not all at once".

docs.title: PLINQ — AsParallel()
docs.text:
// Sequential
var results = numbers.Where(IsPrime).ToList();

// Parallel — one word added
var results = numbers.AsParallel().Where(IsPrime).ToList();

Options:

numbers.AsParallel()
    .WithDegreeOfParallelism(4)
    .WithCancellation(ct)
    .AsOrdered()                    // preserve input order (costs performance)
    .Where(IsPrime)
    .ToList();

⚠️ PLINQ does not preserve order by default. Results come back in whatever order the threads finish. If order matters you need AsOrdered(), which adds buffering and sorting overhead and eats into the benefit.

docs.title: When parallelism actually pays
docs.text:
There is a fixed cost: partitioning the work, spinning up threads, coordinating, and merging results. That cost has to be smaller than what you save.

// ✓ WORTH IT — expensive work, many items
Parallel.ForEach(images, img => ApplyComplexFilter(img));

// ✗ NOT WORTH IT — trivial work, overhead dominates
Parallel.ForEach(numbers, n => n * 2);       // SLOWER than a plain loop

The rough rule: the per-item work needs to be meaningfully more expensive than the coordination overhead, and there need to be enough items to spread across cores. A hundred items of trivial work will be slower in parallel. A hundred thousand items of real computation will be much faster.

Always measure. BenchmarkDotNet exists for exactly this — 19.14.

docs.title: ⚠️ Why this is usually wrong in ASP.NET Core
docs.text:
This is the part interviewers care about.

A web server is already parallel. It is handling many requests at once, spread across all your cores. Those cores are not sitting idle waiting for you to use them.

When one request calls Parallel.ForEach, it grabs threads from the same shared pool that serves every other request. So:

  • One request gets faster.
  • Every other request gets slower, because the pool is now busier.
  • Under load, requests queue and overall throughput drops.

You have optimised one request at the expense of total capacity. On a server, throughput usually matters more than the latency of any single request.

// In a controller — usually the wrong instinct
[HttpPost("process")]
public IActionResult Process(List<Item> items)
{
    Parallel.ForEach(items, ProcessItem);   // steals threads from other requests
    return Ok();
}

When it is defensible: the work is genuinely CPU-heavy, takes seconds, and the endpoint is low-traffic — a nightly report, an admin-only bulk operation. Even then, MaxDegreeOfParallelism should be capped so it cannot consume every core.

The better answer for heavy work is usually to push it out of the request entirely — onto a background service or a queue — so the request returns immediately and the work happens where it cannot hurt request throughput. See 21.1.

docs.title: Never use Parallel.ForEach with async lambdas
docs.text:
// BROKEN — this is async void
Parallel.ForEach(urls, async url => await http.GetStringAsync(url));

Parallel.ForEach takes an Action<T>, so an async lambda becomes async void (2.15). The loop returns immediately with all the work still running, unobserved, and any exception crashes the process.

Use Parallel.ForEachAsync or Task.WhenAll instead.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The three ways to handle a batch, and when each is right:

// 1. I/O-bound, all at once — fine for a handful of items
var results = await Task.WhenAll(ids.Select(id => FetchAsync(id, ct)));

// 2. I/O-bound, throttled — the right answer for hundreds or thousands
var results = new ConcurrentBag<Result>();
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(
    ids,
    new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 10, CancellationToken = ct },
    async (id, token) => results.Add(await FetchAsync(id, token)));

// 3. CPU-bound — genuine parallelism across cores
var results = items
    .AsParallel()
    .WithCancellation(ct)
    .Select(ExpensiveTransform)
    .ToList();

Note the ConcurrentBag in the second example. Writing to a plain List<T> from a parallel loop will corrupt it — see 2.3. This is one of the most common bugs in parallel code:

var results = new List<Result>();
Parallel.ForEach(items, item =>
{
    results.Add(Process(item));      // ✗ RACE — List is not thread-safe
});

The failure is nasty because it is intermittent: sometimes you lose items, sometimes you get a corrupted internal array, sometimes it throws IndexOutOfRangeException from inside Add.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between parallel and asynchronous?

Async is about not blocking a thread while waiting for something external — a network call or a disk read. It does not make the operation faster; it frees the thread to do other work during the wait. Parallel is about using multiple CPU cores to complete a computation sooner. So async is the answer for I/O-bound work and parallelism is the answer for CPU-bound work. Using parallelism for I/O just occupies several threads all doing nothing, which is strictly worse than one async call.

Q: Why is Parallel.ForEach usually wrong in ASP.NET Core?

Because the server is already parallel — it is handling many requests concurrently across all the cores. Threads come from a shared pool, so when one request parallelises, it takes capacity away from every other request. That makes one request faster and everything else slower, and under load overall throughput drops. On a server, total throughput normally matters more than the latency of an individual request. If the work is genuinely heavy, the better answer is to move it out of the request onto a background service or queue.

Q: When does parallelism actually help?

When the work is CPU-bound, there are enough items to spread across cores, and the per-item cost is significantly larger than the coordination overhead. Partitioning, thread management and merging results all cost something, so parallelising trivial work over a small collection is slower than a plain loop. It also has to be work that can be done independently — if every iteration needs a lock on shared state, you have serialised it again and paid the overhead for nothing. And I would always measure rather than assume.

Q: What is Parallel.ForEachAsync for?

It runs asynchronous operations over a collection with a configurable concurrency limit, which is the missing piece between Task.WhenAll and manual throttling. WhenAll over a thousand items starts a thousand operations at once, which exhausts connections and gets you rate-limited. Before .NET 6 you would wrap a SemaphoreSlim around it; now Parallel.ForEachAsync with MaxDegreeOfParallelism does it cleanly. Despite the name it is about controlled concurrency for I/O, not CPU parallelism.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Writing to a List<T> from a parallel loop corrupts it. Use a concurrent collection or collect per-thread results.
  • Parallel.ForEach with an async lambda is async void. Use Parallel.ForEachAsync.
  • PLINQ does not preserve order unless you add AsOrdered(), which costs performance.
  • Parallelism on small or cheap work is slower than sequential, because of coordination overhead.
  • In ASP.NET Core it steals threads from other requests and reduces overall throughput.
  • Exceptions come back wrapped in AggregateException. See 2.16.
  • A lock inside a parallel loop serialises it, so you pay all the overhead and get none of the benefit.
  • Never nest parallel loops. The thread explosion makes it far slower than a single level.

docs.title: 6.3 — Service Lifetimes: Transient, Scoped, Singleton
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 6. Dependency Injection Prev: 6.2 The built-in container · Next: 6.4 Captive dependency

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Transient = a new instance every time it's injected. Scoped = one per HTTP request. Singleton = one for the application's lifetime.
  • The consumer's lifetime wins: a transient injected into a singleton effectively becomes a singleton.
  • DbContext is scoped. Registering it as a singleton is the classic wrong answer — it isn't thread-safe and its change tracker grows forever.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Every service you register with the DI container has to answer one question: when someone asks for this, do I hand back a fresh object or one I made earlier?

That's the entire idea. The three lifetimes are three answers to it, and picking the wrong one produces bugs that don't show up until you have concurrent traffic — which is exactly why interviewers ask about it. It's a question where the wrong answer is invisible in development.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The container tracks instances per scope. A scope is an IServiceScope — a container that lives for a bounded period and disposes everything it created when it ends.

In ASP.NET Core, the framework creates a scope at the start of each HTTP request and disposes it when the response completes. That's why "scoped" and "per request" are used interchangeably in web apps — but they aren't the same thing, and that distinction is the follow-up question. A BackgroundService has no ambient scope, so scoped services must be resolved from a scope you create yourself.

Lifetime Instance per Disposed when Thread safety needed Transient every resolution the owning scope ends no (usually) Scoped scope (= HTTP request) the request ends no Singleton application app shuts down yes

Singletons are shared across concurrent requests. That means any mutable state inside one must be thread-safe — and this is where most singleton bugs actually come from, not from the registration itself.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddTransient<IEmailFormatter, EmailFormatter>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IPricingCache, PricingCache>();

// DbContext is registered scoped by default — this is AddScoped underneath.
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o =>
    o.UseSqlServer(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")));

Proving the behaviour to yourself is worth doing once:

public class LifetimeDemo(
    ITransientService a, ITransientService b,
    IScopedService c,    IScopedService d)
{
    // a.Id != b.Id  — two separate instances
    // c.Id == d.Id  — same instance within this request
    //                 but a different Id on the next request
}

Resolving a scoped service where no scope exists — a BackgroundService, a hosted service, or startup code:

public class OrderCleanupService(IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();
            var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

            await db.Orders
                .Where(o => o.ExpiresAt < DateTimeOffset.UtcNow)
                .ExecuteDeleteAsync(stoppingToken);

            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

The scope must be created inside the loop, not outside it. A scope held for the life of the service is a singleton DbContext wearing a disguise.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Explain the three service lifetimes in ASP.NET Core.

Transient gives you a new instance every time it's resolved, so it's for cheap stateless things. Scoped gives you one instance per scope, and in a web app the framework creates a scope per HTTP request — so it's one per request, which is what you want for a DbContext or anything representing a unit of work. Singleton gives you one instance for the whole application, which is right for caches and configuration, but it means the instance is shared across concurrent requests so any mutable state has to be thread-safe.

Q: What happens if you inject a scoped service into a singleton?

The singleton captures it on first construction and holds it forever, so a request-scoped object becomes application-scoped. With a DbContext that's genuinely bad: it isn't thread-safe, so concurrent requests corrupt its internal state, and its change tracker accumulates every entity it has ever seen, which is a memory leak. The container catches this at startup in development because scope validation is on by default there — but it's off in production, which is the part people miss. If a singleton genuinely needs a scoped service, inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per operation.

Q: Is a transient service ever effectively a singleton?

Yes, and this is the part that surprises people. Lifetime is a property of the object graph, not the registration. If a singleton takes a transient in its constructor, that transient is resolved once and lives as long as the singleton. "Transient" only describes how often the container creates one, not how long the result survives.

Q: Why is DbContext scoped rather than transient?

Because it's a unit of work. You want every repository and service handling a single request to share one context so change tracking and SaveChanges cover the whole operation atomically. Transient would give each consumer its own context and its own separate transaction, which defeats the point.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "Scoped means per class or per controller." It means per scope. In a web request that's per request; outside one there is no ambient scope at all.
  • "The container will stop me registering this wrong." Scope validation is enabled in the Development environment only. The same code can start cleanly in production and fail under load.
  • "Singleton is faster, so prefer it." Only if the object is genuinely shareable and thread-safe. Otherwise you've traded an allocation for a race condition.
  • "AddSingleton(new Thing()) and AddSingleton<Thing>() are equivalent." They aren't for disposal: the container disposes what it creates, so if you hand it an instance you built, you own its lifetime.

docs.title: How to grow this file
docs.text:
Add a question every time one of these happens:

  1. You're asked something in a real or mock interview — write it down the same day, verbatim, before you rewrite it in your head into something you answered well
  2. You read a note and think "how would this get asked?"
  3. You fumble a follow-up — the follow-up is the real question, not the original

Aim for roughly one question per 🔥 topic. That's about 120 questions, which is a realistic target over the full study period and far more useful than a downloaded list of 500 you've never spoken aloud.

docs.title: Drill format
docs.text:
Solo: cover the answers, work through one section, mark every fumble in PROGRESS.md under Weak spots.

With a partner: hand them this file. Ask them to pick randomly and to always ask "why?" once after your answer. The follow-up is where interviews are actually won and lost — a confident first answer followed by silence when probed is worse than a hesitant answer that survives two levels of "why."

Out loud, alone: record yourself. Painful, effective. You will hear the filler words and the places where you trail off, and you can't hear either while you're speaking.

docs.title: System Design Practice
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Topic 25.5 🔥 🎯

System design rounds are increasingly common for mid-level .NET roles and standard for senior. They are not testing whether you know the "right" architecture — they're testing whether you ask about constraints before you draw boxes.

docs.title: The method (use this every time)
docs.text:
1. Clarify requirements — functional and non-functional. Never start drawing first. Ask about scale, read/write ratio, consistency needs, latency budget.
  2. Estimate — requests per second, storage growth, bandwidth. Rough is fine; showing you think in numbers is the point.
  3. Define the API — endpoints and their contracts. This forces concrete thinking.
  4. Data model — entities, relationships, and the access patterns that drive the schema.
  5. High-level design — draw the boxes. Client, gateway, services, data stores, queues.
  6. Deep dive — the interviewer picks a component. Be ready for any of them.
  7. Bottlenecks and scale — where does this break at 10×? What do you fix first?
  8. Tradeoffs — say out loud what you gave up and why.

Step 1 is the one candidates skip and the one interviewers score hardest. Jumping to a diagram before establishing constraints is the most common failure in this round.

docs.title: Worked examples to write
docs.text:
Each gets its own file in this folder. Write them out fully — a design you've written is one you can improvise from; one you've only read is not.

  • [ ] URL shortener — hashing, collisions, redirect performance, analytics
  • [ ] E-commerce checkout — inventory reservation, payment idempotency, order saga
  • [ ] Notification service — fan-out, delivery guarantees, retries, dead lettering
  • [ ] Rate limiter — algorithms (token bucket, sliding window), distributed state
  • [ ] File upload service — presigned URLs, chunking, virus scanning, CDN
  • [ ] Chat / real-time feed — SignalR, backplane, presence, message ordering
  • [ ] Multi-tenant SaaS API — tenant isolation, per-tenant data, noisy neighbours
  • [ ] Job scheduler — durability, exactly-once-ish semantics, poison messages
  • [ ] Audit log service — write volume, immutability, retention, query patterns
  • [ ] Read-heavy product catalog — caching layers, invalidation, search

docs.title: .NET-specific things to bring up
docs.text:
These are what make it an ASP.NET Core system design round rather than a generic one. Working one or two in naturally shows depth:

  • IHttpClientFactory + Polly for service-to-service resilience → 19.11
  • HybridCache or Redis for the caching layer → 19.3
  • Background processing: BackgroundService vs Hangfire vs a queue consumer → 21.1, 21.3
  • Outbox pattern for reliable event publishing from EF Core → 23.8
  • YARP as gateway/BFF → 23.10
  • Health checks driving Kubernetes probes → 18.5, 24.6
  • OpenTelemetry for cross-service tracing → 18.7
  • Stateless app servers so you can scale horizontally → 24.12

docs.title: Numbers worth knowing
docs.text:
Rough orders of magnitude. Precision isn't the point — being able to estimate at all is.

Latency In-memory cache read ~100 ns Redis round trip (same DC) ~0.5–1 ms Database query (indexed, same DC) ~1–10 ms Cross-region round trip ~50–150 ms Disk seek (SSD) ~0.1 ms Scale One well-tuned ASP.NET Core instance thousands of req/s for simple endpoints 1M requests/day ~12 req/s average, plan for 5–10× peak 1 KB per row × 100M rows ~100 GB
